contracts.title: 10.24 · An increment carries a risk line (its tier, rating, depth, radius, depth flags, the live stories it touches and the day read), set and cleared by an edit; a value out of range or a story that is not one is refused with nothing written

10.25 · An increment is parked already waiting for the owner, its note written in the parking's one write; a wait the owner-wait rules refuse, two for one releaser, or one on an increment born closed is refused with nothing written
contracts.description: So owner-action work is never open, claimable work in the moments between parking and setting its wait (friction_e0d993bc1c07).

contracts.title: 10.26 · An open increment drops one pending change by its record, with a reason, its history saying so and the live plan left as it was; a record it holds no change for, or a closed increment, is refused with nothing written

10.27 · An apply cut off part-way leaves pending only the changes it had not applied; the gate reads none its own increment applied as stale, and the next apply, under any of the increment's pull requests, finishes the rest
contracts.description: The merge hook applies a merged increment's pending changes inside its own deadline; PR #145's merge was cut after 20 of increment_fc3a008fe1c6's 76 changes, and because the increment's list was cleared only at the end, the 20 applied changes stayed pending and read stale at the next branch's gate (friction_d7b0fbf11254). Each change now leaves the list as it applies, and a change whose record's latest entry is its own increment's mark, under any of its pull requests, reads applied, not stale.

capabilities.title: 11 · Waits
capabilities.description: An arc waits on an arc, and an increment on an increment on any arc, each with a reason. A loop across both kinds is refused when it is written. The library alone answers whether a wait holds (`waitHolds`), naming its blockers and saying when one can never release.

contracts.title: 11.1 · An increment wait holds until the blocker closes as landed. A failed, withdrawn or missing blocker holds for good, and says it will never release.
11.3 · A wait that would close a loop across arcs and increments is refused, naming the loop, and nothing is written.
11.2 · An arc wait holds until that arc closes.
11.4 · `waitHolds(id)` returns the blockers still holding, each with its reason.

11.5 · holds() answers every live arc's and open increment's wait holds, and every open increment's owner holds, in one reading, each the same as waitHolds and heldOnQuestion give; closed increments have no holds and are omitted.
11.6 · An increment waits for the owner or an outside event with a note: an owner wait holds until cleared, an event wait until its check-back day, then reads passed
contracts.description: ADR-0938 D1. At most one note per releaser; an event wait needs a check-back day not before today, an owner wait takes none; a closed increment waits for nothing. holds() gives them as waitsFor, each with whether it still holds.

reported.note: waits.test.ts 11.6 passes on memory and Postgres.

contracts.title: 11.8 · A wait is cleared from the record that stores it as its blocker lands (an increment) or closes (an arc), with the reason in its history; a failed or withdrawn blocker's wait stays
contracts.description: No stored wait is ever stale, so no front door holds a stale-wait rule (owner, question_86dc1b3f26e3, option A). Cleared in the same step as the close, settle or retire that ends the blocker; the waiter's history keeps the wait.

contracts.title: 11.9 · An arc waits on an increment of another arc
contracts.description: An arc may wait on an increment of another arc: the wait holds the arc and its open work until that increment lands, is cleared when it does, and holds for good if it is withdrawn. An arc waiting on its own increment is a loop and is refused.

contracts.title: 11.10 · An owner wait needs a why (what it protects or unblocks) and may carry a rank, a whole number, 1 first; each write stamps the day it was read again, and writing it again keeps the note, why and rank not given; an event wait takes neither
contracts.description: increment_a513c3fa4117 (arc_e1a8aa255113, research_fb58291956ab sections 3 and 4). An owner wait written without a why, or with a rank that is not a whole number from 1, is refused with nothing written, through addWaitFor and through an increment born waiting (10.25); an event wait with a why or a rank is refused. The stored `reviewed` day is the library's, set to today on every write, and is what `arc waits --audit` reads for a lapsed review. Waits stored before this have no why, rank or review day, and still read.

capabilities.title: 12 · Owner questions
capabilities.description: A question is raised on an arc, with its stakes, statement, context and options, and settled with the owner's answer, which stays on the arc. An increment held on an open question reads as waiting on him (`heldOnQuestion`), and the library alone answers that.

contracts.title: 12.1 · A question is raised with its required fields, and is open.
12.2 · Settling needs an answer and keeps it, with the date and the decision that carried it. A settled question stays readable on its arc.

12.3 · An open increment held on an open question reads as waiting on the owner. Settling the question takes it off every increment's heldOn, keeping their other holds. A question that does not exist holds nothing.
12.4 · A question an increment is held on cannot be retired through retire; retireQuestion (12.9) is the step that releases its holders.

12.5 · An open question carries a review date and a lease, 7 days unless given. It checks fresh until the lease runs out and lapsed after, it is listed as lapsed until renewed, and renewing re-stamps it.
12.6 · Renewing a settled question is refused and nothing is written. A settled question checks settled and is never listed as lapsed.

12.7 · An open question's wording (title, stakes, statement, context, options, analogy, diagram, recommendation) can be corrected in place, changing only the named fields. Its arc, lifecycle, answer and lease are not edited this way, and editing a settled question is refused with nothing written: its answer stands.
12.8 · A question raised on a parked arc is refused, naming the arc, and nothing is written; once its wake day passes, it is raised
contracts.description: ADR-0835 D1: what a session would have asked goes into the arc's residue instead, to be raised when the arc is unparked.

contracts.title: 12.9 · Retiring a question with retireQuestion takes it off the heldOn of every increment held on it, open or closed (keeping their other holds), and retires it in one step, naming the increments released. A record that is not a live question is refused with nothing written.
12.10 · An open question carries the session putting it to the owner, set and cleared in place through editQuestion; settling clears it, and a settled question cannot carry one
contracts.description: So two sessions never put the same open question to the owner at once (friction_1e1a7ce50de1); whether the marking session is still live is the agent link's reading (its 5.36).

contracts.title: 12.11 · an open question moves to another arc in place, keeping its id, wording and holders
contracts.description: moveQuestion changes an open question's arc, recording the reason in its history; a parked target takes it (it parks with the arc, ADR-0835 D2), a closed or missing arc, the same arc, or a settled question is refused with nothing written.

capabilities.title: 13 · Decision log
capabilities.description: Decision numbers do not collide, even across concurrent writers, and history reserves every number a decision has held. Other projects start at 1. In the project named exactly `storytree`, automatic numbers exceed the persisted floor and every number any non-health record has ever held; automatic numbering is refused if that setting is absent. An explicit free number remains accepted. The N1 move is complete: the 29 Full record decisions retain their 0.2 numbers, the floor is 662, and the 53 founding books are ADR-0663..0715. Ordinary edits cannot change or remove a decision's number. A decision's status is proposed or accepted, and it can be superseded: the superseded decision is kept, and reads as superseded. A decision carries the load-bearing mark, who decided it, in their own words, and one composed statement. Health events never reserve decision numbers, including in repair previews and writes; legacy non-health reservations remain.

contracts.title: 13.1 · In projects with automatic numbering, decisions recorded at once from separate connections get distinct numbers, each higher than any before. A number held by another decision is never reused, including retired decisions and old numbers kept in history. Ordinary edits cannot change or remove a decision's number and a refused edit writes nothing.
13.2 · A decision is superseded exactly when an accepted decision names it in `supersedes`. It stays readable, and a supersession loop is refused.
13.3 · Status and the load-bearing mark are stored and read back, and a decision written before status was is upgraded to carry one.
13.4 · A decision may carry one composed statement. A read returns it marked stale when the decision's text changed after it was written, and the full text is always readable.

13.5 · Only in the storytree project, numberDecision repairs a live decision once to the number in its own single Full record: ADR-NNNN line. Missing or ambiguous lines, mismatches, retired records, previous repairs, and numbers any non-health record has ever held are refused without writing. Concurrent repairs cannot share a number or repair a record twice. The old number stays in history; editNote still refuses number. decisionNumberPlan lists proposed old → new numbers and refusals, including duplicate targets, without writing. Decisions without a Full record line are untouched. Health events never reserve decision numbers, including in repair previews and writes; legacy non-health reservations remain.

13.6 · Only in storytree, setDecisionNumberFloor previews by default and apply: true stores 0.2's final number once as a positive safe integer project setting, retained in history and snapshots. Repeated or lower floor settings are refused, including concurrent attempts. Recording without an explicit number is refused while the floor is unset; afterwards, automatic numbers exceed the floor and every number any non-health record has ever held, with concurrent writers receiving distinct numbers. An explicit free number remains accepted; other projects still auto-number from 1. Health events never reserve decision numbers, including in repair previews and writes; legacy non-health reservations remain.

13.7 · numberDecisionsFromFullRecord previews by default; apply: true applies every eligible proposal through numberDecision and returns each refusal. Decisions already matching their Full record number are omitted. Duplicate targets are refused, the write checks history again under the project lock, and repeated bulk application writes nothing once all eligible repairs are complete.

13.8 · Only in storytree with its floor set, numberFoundingDecisions previews live decisions that existed at switch-on and have no Full record line, in first-creation history order. Targets exceed the floor and every number any non-health record has ever held. Preview writes and reserves nothing; apply: true rechecks every write and returns each refusal. The record keeps its identity, other fields and old number in history. Concurrent moves cannot share numbers or move a book twice. Completed moves, Full record decisions and decisions created after switch-on are omitted; a repeat can finish a partial run without renumbering completed books. Health events never reserve decision numbers, including in repair previews and writes; legacy non-health reservations remain.
13.9 · `decisions()` gives every live decision's view in one reading, oldest first, each the same as `decision(id)` gives.

13.10 · The library declares the `adr` family the command line lists 4th: a pulled decision pushed back unedited writes nothing and never asks for the writer, and an edited title writes that field alone
contracts.description: The decision log's verbs (new, pull, push, compose, list) are declared beside the library's own commands (ADR-1033, ADR-1077 D2) and mounted by the command line at their place, with the adr guesses; a push hands the library only what changed.

capabilities.title: 14 · Ranked search
capabilities.description:
A library search ranks the live artifacts by how close their meaning is to the question, using an embedding model (Snowflake's arctic-embed-s, ADR-1115; bge-small until 2026-10-22) run on this computer, with no LLM, paid API or extra service, as the owner directed (0.2's ADR-0664). An artifact written or edited is embedded again before the next search ranks it, and with no model to hand the search falls back to word matches and says why.

As built: Windows delivery stages the locked Transformers Node distribution, ONNX Runtime CPU binding and DLL, and the Sharp runtime dependency beside the CLI and MCP entrypoints for x64 and arm64. No model weights ship. The existing lazy loader downloads arctic-embed-s on first use into <storytree home>/models, from one pinned revision, checking each file's SHA-256. The installed-layout check imports Transformers and runs a weight-free ONNX Identity graph on the native CPU backend without a source checkout. Windows x64 execution is checked by installer CI; ARM64 PE headers are inspected, with ARM64 execution awaiting a native Windows acceptance run.

contracts.title: 14.1 · `rank(query)` orders the live artifacts by meaning, best first, with each one's score, and finds an artifact that shares no word with the question.

14.2 · An artifact scores by its best chunk (its rendered text packed into chunks of at most 1600 characters on paragraph boundaries, ADR-1044 D1), and at most `limit` artifacts come back, ten unless told.

14.3 · An edited artifact ranks by its new words at the next search; a chunk already embedded is not embedded again, and a library opened afresh on the same project reads the kept vectors, embedding only the question.
14.4 · With no embedding model to hand (switched off, or it cannot load), `rank` gives the word matches of `search` and says why, rather than failing.

14.5 · The installed Windows CLI and MCP tools resolve their bundled Transformers and native ONNX CPU runtime without a checkout or npm installation, on x64 and arm64. The installer ships runtime code and target binaries, never model weights; the embedding model remains a first-use download into <storytree home>/models.

14.7 · A ranked search puts first the records it names by title: one whose title (a definition's term) is the search, ignoring case, spacing and a leading contract number; then one whose contract number (such as 7.17) is a word of the search; then one whose title holds every word of it as a whole word, ignoring case, a plural finding its singular, never letters inside a longer word; each group, and the rest, keep their meaning order.

14.8 · rankAll ranks live stories, capabilities and contracts by their own wording alongside knowledge artifacts, labels each hit with its type, and finds a contract whose meaning matches even when it shares no query word.

14.9 · With no embedding model, rankAll returns word matches including a contract holding every query word, reports why it fell back, and never treats a plan record’s parent identifier as searchable words.

14.10 · Ranked searches reuse local vectors across processes only within the same server, project database identity and model. Only missing content keys come from Postgres, including after one note is added. Other servers, projects, recreated databases and old unscoped entries cannot alter ranks or scores. Writes reach Postgres and the scoped local copy; concurrent processes share it safely, and no identity or usable local storage falls back to Postgres.

14.11 · An explicit literal phrase lookup matches case-sensitive contiguous text within stored top-level string fields of selected artifact and plan kinds, returns full live records in id order with bounded pages and a continuation cursor, sees edits and retirement, and filters before records leave Postgres. Ranked search is unchanged.
14.12 · A long note's late paragraph is embedded: each chunk fits the 512 tokens the model reads, so a search finds the note by what that paragraph says
contracts.description: bge-small reads only its first 512 tokens and drops the rest without warning; chunks of at most about 1,600 characters keep every part of a note inside what it reads (ADR-1044 D1).

contracts.title: 14.13 · Behind a proxy that HTTPS_PROXY or HTTP_PROXY names, the embedding model's first-use download goes through that proxy (NO_PROXY honoured), and a failed load behind a proxy names the hosts the proxy must allow
contracts.description: A cloud container reaches the internet only through its agent proxy, and Node's fetch ignores HTTPS_PROXY, so without this the download fails and search ranks by words (friction_84c6d7d08f35).

contracts.title: 14.14 · The embedding model loads only from one pinned revision, and only files whose SHA-256 matches the hashes committed in the repo; a file that differs, or one the pinned model does not list, is deleted and the load refused naming it (with both hashes), so search falls back to words and says why
contracts.description: Supply-chain guard for bge-small (research_6bd2bb78600a): no moving `main`, no trust-on-first-download. Checked after a download and once per cached copy.

contracts.title: 14.15 · A question is embedded with the model's query prefix, and an artifact's chunks never are
contracts.description: Snowflake's arctic-embed-s, library search's model since question_80102d5cea6e, is trained to read a search question after "Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: " and a passage with nothing before it. A ranked search sends the question with the embedder's query prefix and every chunk without it.

capabilities.title: 15 · Connection by address
capabilities.description: Instead of the local app's Postgres or Cloud SQL with Google sign-in, storytree reaches any Postgres by its address (Neon, Supabase, RDS, self-hosted, Cloud SQL with an ordinary user), its password resolved as a key.

contracts.title: 15.1 · A library at a Postgres address, with its password saved as the `postgres` key, opens, writes and reads a project as a password-authenticated role.
contracts.description: Proven against the throwaway test server with a role that must give its password (scram-sha-256).

contracts.title: 15.2 · With no password saved for the library (no `postgres` key and no PGPASSWORD), connecting is refused saying so and how to save one, before anything reaches the server.
15.3 · A password the server refuses and a host that cannot be reached are each refused as their own problem, with what to fix, and never show the password.
15.4 · A remote address gets the password only after its certificate is checked
contracts.description: ADR-0943 D1, narrowed by ADR-0997 D1: a library at a non-local address connects only over TLS whose certificate chains to a trust anchor storytree was given (the address's sslrootcert when it names one, otherwise Node's authorities alone; no build trusts a certificate of storytree's own), or, when the address names sslrootcert, is exactly one of the certificates that file holds (compared on the whole certificate, and in date), and names the host it dialled; otherwise it is refused before any password is sent, on the admin pool and every project's. This holds alike under Node's runtime and the desktop app's Electron, whose TLS does not take a self-signed certificate that is no authority as a trust anchor. A plain-text password request is refused even over TLS, and no sslmode or connection-string override weakens it.

contracts.title: 15.5 · The routed library's connection string, signed in with its key, reaches the database it names, for psql; it stores nothing, and no saved password or a Cloud SQL library is refused saying why
contracts.description: `storytree auth connection [--database <name>]` prints the library routing names as a postgres:// URL carrying the `postgres` key's password (a local url as it is), so a hand script runs psql "$(storytree auth connection --database storytree-activity)" in one call (friction_80b5888ce8a0).

stories.title: Session management
stories.description: Session management keeps the record of who is doing what, so the user's own Claude Code or Codex can work on a storytree project and be seen doing it. A passive layer of hooks records what every agent does, so even an agent that ignores storytree shows up as unplanned activity; sessions, claims and the context reading are read from that record. It also keeps the runs a session started (capabilities 12 to 16, Process ledger's until it folded in): who started each, sight of those whose request ended, what remains on this computer, stopping only the caller's own, and an honest inventory at the session's end, so a session clears its own runs before it closes. Owns packages/session-management and packages/processes (ADR-1066 D3). Which project a folder is and the user's settings are Project and caller's (packages/project-and-caller, ADR-1025), which this story stands on. Named Session management rather than Sessions, which is an overloaded term (ADR-0969 D4); until 2026-10-11 it was The agent link. The agent's tools are served by the MCP server story, whose wrapper calls what this story exports to name the caller, record the call and end merged claims (ADR-0969 D1). Registering the hooks, the setup check, making a folder a project and wiring the pipeline belong to The app setup (ADR-0969 D3). Red-green is a convention the habits card teaches, not a loop storytree runs.

capabilities.title: 2 · Agent activity log
capabilities.description: Session management's own logbook of what agents do, one per project and kept beside the library rather than inside it, with one line for each thing that happens: a session starts or ends, a file is edited, a command runs, an artifact is read, work is claimed, released or landed. Lines are only ever added, never changed, and can be read back in order as "everything since line N", including lines that other processes wrote.

capabilities.title: 3 · Hooks
capabilities.description: Small commands that Claude Code and Codex run by themselves when a session starts, after every file edit, before and after every shell command, at the end of each turn, and when it ends, each adding one line about that session to the agent activity log, so an agent that never calls storytree still shows up. At each prompt, one more adds the project's definitions for the terms the prompt names, for the agent to read: every matching term not yet given this session, longest first, with no cap (3.7). The cap of five that 0.2's ADR-0201 set, never measured and never chosen by the owner, is removed by the owner's named choice ("turn the cap off.", 2026-09-28; ADR-0739 D3, ADR-0633); the once-per-session and harness-notice rules, which 0.2 did measure, stay. The same prompt hook carries capability 9's fresh-session nudge to a Claude Code session past its context guidance (9.9). At a session's start in a folder that isn't a storytree project yet, the harness waits for one more (Codex's own start hook, a second one for Claude Code), which has the agent ask the user whether to set storytree up there before the task it was given, and sets nothing up itself (8.12). Every hook also records the transcript path the harness named for its session, so capability 9 can work out any session's tokens used when asked, never from a transcript found by folder (ADR-0725, ADR-0728). They run in the background and always exit cleanly, so they can never slow down or break the agent, and when storytree isn't running they do nothing.

contracts.title: 3.1 · Real, recorded Claude Code hook inputs (a start, a file edit, a shell command, an end) are fed in, and four lines appear on that session, carrying the file path, the command and the machine's name.
3.2 · The same holds for real, recorded Codex hook inputs, where the edited files are read out of its patch text.
3.3 · With storytree stopped, with garbage input, or outside a storytree project, the command exits cleanly in under half a second and writes nothing.
3.4 · It runs on Windows without a Unix shell, and it never prints anything the agent would see.

3.5 · Real, recorded hook inputs for starting a subagent, for a storytree tool call made inside it, and for one made by the orchestrator make three lines: the subagent's id, type and task; the subagent asking, by its id and type, with the call's id; and the orchestrator asking, with its call's id. The same holds for Claude Code and for Codex.

3.6 · Real, recorded hook inputs from before a shell command, after one that failed, and at the end of a turn make three lines: the command started and the command finished, both under the call's id, and the turn ended. For Codex, whose hooks the agent waits for, the hook hands its line to one in the background and exits.

3.7 · At each prompt, the project's definitions for the terms it names are added for the agent: whole words in any case or plural, every one not yet given this session, longest first, with no cap (a prompt naming six gets all six), each once a session, each meaning's first line cut to 200 characters. A definition answers only to a name that points at it alone: its term unless another definition has the same term, a "/"-part only when no other definition answers to it. A harness's own notice, or an agent's message (a subagent's report, another session's message), gets none, and with storytree stopped nothing is printed.

3.8 · The status line shows what this session holds, how many other agents are working, and a warning when another is editing a file it edited. With storytree stopped it says so, and outside a project it shows nothing.

3.12 · Real, recorded Claude Code and Codex hook inputs record on their session the transcript path the harness named (`transcript_path`), and a session's transcript reads as the latest one recorded for it. For a `claude -p` run whose transcript sits under a project directory unrelated to its `cwd`, and for a session whose `cwd` is now worktree B while its transcript sits under the project directory of folder A where it started, it is exactly the named path; no folder is searched.

3.13 · Each hook streams its session's new transcript records, and each subagent's (from <transcript>/subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl) under its parent session by the subagent's id, into the shared log, secrets scrubbed (9.12), from where the last hook left off (a cursor read from the store), only whole records, never twice, and at most 2 MB per hook (ADR-0749 D3, D4).

3.14 · Lines a hook writes while storytree cannot be reached (not running, the store refusing, or the store too slow to take them before the hook's deadline cuts it off) wait on this machine under the storytree home, each with the time and machine it was written at; the next hook that reaches the log uploads them before its own, oldest first, at their own times, and each line exactly once, however many hooks try (ADR-0749 consequences).

3.15 · Real, recorded prompt inputs make a prompt line on their session (without the prompt's words), for Claude Code and Codex alike, and a Claude Code Stop always makes a turn-ended line carrying how many background tasks are still running (ADR-0754 D5).
3.16 · Every line a hook writes records the git branch its folder is on (even one with no commit yet), beside the folder; a folder on no branch records none (ADR-0754 D4).

3.17 · When a turn ends with its session's work resolved and no standing close-out, the Stop hook's output reminds the agent to close out; a session that is idle or has exited is never prompted (ADR-0758 D4).

3.19 · A Claude Code session's end is recorded even though Claude Code stops its end hook after 1.5 s and the store takes longer than that to answer: run as setup registers it (with `--background`) and cut short at 1.5 s, the hook hands its line to a copy of itself that outlives it, and the session-ended line lands.

3.18 · A Codex hook that runs, in any folder, notes on this machine that Codex runs storytree's hooks; they read as waiting while registered and not yet run since, and a later registration reads as waiting again.

reported.note: codex-trust.test.ts: red first (expected running, got waiting: no hook noted it), green after runHook notes Codex hooks.

contracts.title: 3.21 · A hook's reads do not grow with the log's length: the same hooks (a command's finish, which also hands on the look around the machine, a prompt, and the status line) take about as much from the store in a project whose log holds weeks of history as in one whose log holds an hour's.

contracts.title: 3.22 · After a shell command, changed tracked and non-ignored files in its Git worktree are recorded as edits for that session, including repeated writes, additions, deletions and moves. Pre-existing dirt, read-only commands, staging, unchanged commits, and files left as a pull, merge, checkout, switch, reset or rebase wrote them invent no edits. Explicit edit hooks advance the baseline; failed commands and offline hooks retain their writes.
3.23 · A failing hook leaves a local trace
3.24 · A hook cut off at its deadline while a statement of its waits on the server leaves no statement running there: the server ends it

3.37 · The prompt hook records a yes the user sends as the allow command
