capabilities.title: 4 · Sessions
capabilities.description: Reads the agent activity log as a list of agent sessions, one per Claude Code or Codex window, each showing which of the two it is, which folder it works in, when it started and when it was last seen. A session is working from a prompt until its turn ends, or while a command it started runs, and waiting otherwise (ADR-0754 D5); ended once its end line arrives. A session whose hooks report no turns (no prompt line: hooks not running, or installed before D5) is working while its lines keep arriving and waiting after the quiet time, the user's `idle-after` setting (capability 10, 10.10; ADR-0739 D2), 30 minutes when unset. So it never reads as working just because nobody said otherwise.

contracts.title: 4.1 · A start line makes a working session labelled "Claude Code", with its folder, when it started and when it was last seen.
4.2 · A session whose hooks report no turns reads as waiting once no line has come for longer than the quiet time, and after its end line it reads as ended.
4.3 · A resumed window continues the same session instead of starting a second one.
4.4 · A Codex session whose hooks never ran, but which calls a storytree tool, still appears and is flagged "hooks not running", so a missing hook never looks like an agent doing nothing.

4.5 · A command that started 40 minutes ago and has not finished keeps its session working. Once it finishes, or its turn ends with no background task left running, it no longer counts, and one started longer ago than the longest a command may run no longer counts.

4.6 · A session is its harness session id, never a folder: one whose lines name two folders reads with both as its worktrees, in the order it first worked in each, while its folder stays the one it started in (ADR-0749 D2).

4.7 · A session with no line for longer than a command may run (12 hours) and no end line has stopped reporting: it reads as gone, never as ended, since nothing said it ended; up to that limit it reads as idle (ADR-0749 consequences).

4.8 · Working comes from turn state (ADR-0754 D5): a prompt makes its session working until its turn ends, however long the turn writes no line, and compacting mid-turn does not end it; its end makes it waiting at once; a turn that ends with background tasks still running leaves their command running, so the session stays working until it finishes.

4.9 · Who is listed (ADR-0754 D4): a session whose branches (every branch other than main its lines name, a merged line's excepted) still hold open work stays listed whatever its end line or silence says; once its work resolves (the latest branch-state line for each branch says resolved), a session leaves on its end line or after the leave-after quiet time, counted from its last line or the resolution, whichever is later; a session the Claude or Codex app keeps (a session-archived or session-unarchived line names it) shows done instead of leaving, is removed at once when archived, and comes back when un-archived.

4.10 · Each branch a session worked on is marked resolved once a pull request from it merged (asked of GitHub from any machine), or, on the machine it was worked on, once it has nothing ahead of the main line or is deleted (a branch with no commit yet is neither); one still ahead stays open, and one worked on again after it resolved is looked at again and reads open when it is ahead. A branch-state line is written only when the state changes, on the session that saw it (ADR-0754 D4). The hooks take this look once a minute through a copy of themselves that may run longer than a hook, so a merge is recorded though GitHub answers later than a hook may run. A claim's `merged` line resolves its branch as a branch-state line does, until a later look reads it open.

4.11 · Closing out records whether the session says it is safe to close and why, releases every capability and increment claim it still holds regardless of branch or whether a tool or edit hook took it, and returns the released ids. Other sessions keep their claims; repeating close-out releases nothing. Verification of safe still checks unfinished work and runs.

4.12 · A yes is checked, never trusted: it leaves the list at once when its branches are resolved and nothing of its own runs; otherwise it stays and needs you, naming the disagreement; a no stays with its why; a later prompt or new admitted claim voids it (ADR-0758 D3). Closing out first asks whether the project’s branches have merged, so a merge no hook recorded still bears a yes out.

4.25 · The sessions the Claude desktop app and Codex keep are read, read-only, from their own files on each machine (Claude's claude-code-sessions/<account>/<org>/local_*.json: cliSessionId and isArchived; Codex's state_5.sqlite threads: id and archived, headless runs and subagents excluded), and each session the project's log knows gets a session-archived or session-unarchived line when its state there changes, never otherwise. Absent files read as absent and damaged ones as unreadable, and neither writes anything (ADR-0754 D4).

4.13 · The sessions listing (`storytree session list`) first asks whether the project's branches have merged, so it never waits on a hook to have recorded a merge, then shows each session the list shows, one block each, with its state, listing, folder, open and resolved branches, its work on main as its flag or label (4.26), close-out and what needs you; a hidden one (a verified close-out) only with --all; --json gives the same sessions as data.

4.18 · The hooks reap a worktree once it can go (ADR-0790): a clean linked worktree whose head is in the main line, whose every session (at least one) has a verified close-out or is archived, which is not locked and holds neither the hook's folder nor a registered hook script, is removed and unregistered and its branch deleted; a dirty, unmerged, locked, unused, still-used, protected or hook-running one stays; its folder is moved to a trash folder first and the trash emptied out of the hook's way.

4.19 · How the app that keeps a session names and describes it reaches the log: for each session this project knows, the Claude desktop app's title and its post-turn summary's status, or Codex's thread name (else its title), are written as one `session-described` line (by whichever session read the records, never on the session it is about), scrubbed as transcripts are and held to 120 and 300 characters, and written again only when those words change. Each session read from the log carries the latest title and status.

4.20 · A line about other sessions (a claim's merge, a branch's state, what an app keeps or how it names a session) never makes its writer a session: a person, or the app, that only looked is not listed, and an agent's look does not count as its own work.

4.21 · The app looks at each project's branches itself, once a minute while it runs, asking from the latest folder this machine still has and writing under app:<machine>, so its sessions list never waits on a hook to have recorded a merge.

4.22 · A session reads, for each folder its lines name, the branches recorded there, in the order first recorded, with whether each still holds open work and, while open, its pull request as the latest look read it (4.24). The main line is no branch; a branch with no folder is placed in the folder the session last worked in.

4.23 · A session reads the commands it started and has not seen finish, each with its command text and start time, background ones a turn left running included: the same reading that keeps a session working (4.5, 4.8).

4.24 · The branch look reads every open pull request of the project's repository in one GitHub call, alongside its merged-pull-request call, under the same once-a-minute stamp and fail-soft rules: for each open branch, its number, whether it is a draft, its head commit's checks taken together (pending, passing or failing; none when it has none), and whether it waits in the merge queue. The branch-state line carries these and is written again only when one changes; GitHub not answering erases nothing; a pull request closed unmerged leaves the branch open with none. The Session reading carries them on each open branch in branchesByFolder.

4.26 · Work on main is never silently dropped (ADR-0906): a session that edited files inside a folder on the main line while the latest look on its machine finds that folder's main uncommitted, or that holds an increment it claimed on main, stays listed whatever its end or silence, flagged "worked on main, outside a workspace"; while the repository has no commit yet it is labelled "setting up git, first commit pending" instead; a yes close-out is not verified while the flag stands; once the work is committed (and the claim gone) the flag goes and it leaves as 4.9 says. A file edited outside the folder, or a capability claimed on main, raises no flag.

4.27 · The branch look (4.10) also looks, on this machine, at each folder a session edited files in, or claimed an increment in, while on the main line: it writes a main-state line saying whether that folder's main holds uncommitted changes and whether its repository has no commit yet, only when that changes, under the same once-a-minute stamp and fail-soft rules; a folder no longer on the main line reads as holding none.

4.28 · The sessions read from the lines that decide them, and the claims read from those standing, are what a fold of the whole log gives at any time, from a share of its lines; the list's own read leaves out only sessions the list hides, and the status line's states agree.

reported.note: Passes on main since #668.

contracts.title: 4.29 · A session last seen on its machine before that machine's recorded start reads gone, not working, to a reader on any machine, with no command running, and its claims read free; one seen since the start, or on another machine, reads as before

4.30 · The first hook on a machine to reach a project's log after the machine starts records that start there, once: a later hook reading the same start a moment apart writes nothing; the next start, or another project, is recorded again
4.32 · A session in a harness storytree has no hooks for reads as connected in the sessions list, never flagged hooks not running; a watched harness's session without hooks still is
4.33 · A project's folder is its marker's folder, even when its sessions worked in a subfolder
4.34 · Naming a session, closing it out and listing the sessions are verbs declared once: closing out or naming answers in the same sentence for either door, writing to the calling session's log
4.35 · The hook times read back by harness, event and machine

4.36 · The hooks sweep worktree folders git no longer lists (ADR-0790 D4): an idle one under .claude/worktrees whose every unignored file git already has is removed, its links removed and never followed; one holding content git lacks, one a live process works in, or one a session wrote in lately stays.

4.37 · A worktree the hooks reap while a test Postgres still runs on its .pgtest/data has that server stopped first (its postmaster.pid checked to name a live Postgres process) and the folder removed.
4.38 · A pool lane-failed or lane-reoffered line makes no session read live
4.39 · The branch-state look's git calls learn this machine's speed, floored at 2 s and capped at 5 s

capabilities.title: 5 · Claims
capabilities.description: Before building a capability, the agent claims it with a one-line reason, so the user and the other agents can see who is on what, and every edit its session makes while holding the claim counts toward that capability. Only one live session can hold a capability: a second agent is refused with the holder's name and picks other work instead of queueing, and a claim ends when the agent lands or releases it, when its session ends, or when another agent takes it over after the holder has gone idle.

contracts.title: 5.1 · Session A claims "email form", and the claim shows A and the reason.

5.2 · A second live claimant is refused naming the holder and why it still binds, including any unverified close-out disagreement; a claim-refused line records the refusal. An idle holder, including one whose standing safe close-out is verified against its branches and running work, permits takeover even with stale command telemetry. A prompt, admitted claim or non-compaction restart voids that close-out.
5.3 · When A reports it landed, the claim ends and a "landed" line is written. A release, or A's session ending, also ends it.
5.4 · A claim on a capability the library doesn't have is refused, and when two agents claim at the same instant exactly one wins.
5.5 · An edit made while A holds "email form" counts toward it, and an edit from a session holding nothing counts as unplanned activity.
5.6 · While a command A started is still running, past the quiet time, B's claim on A's capability is refused, naming A.

reported.note: 37 existing claims/workspace/activity tests pass, including single-history-scan refusal, exclusivity, running-owner liveness, restart takeover, attribution, waits and cancellation. Red and green logs retained under /tmp/st03-claim-latency-evidence.

contracts.title: 5.7 · Session A claims a proposed increment, and the claim shows A and the reason while the library shows the increment active; B's claim on it is refused, naming A. An active one is not started again, and a closed one is refused.

5.8 · Claiming an increment whose own wait holds, or whose arc's wait holds, is refused, naming each blocker and its reason, and one held on an open question is refused as waiting on the owner. Nothing is written and the increment is not started. Once the wait releases, the claim succeeds.
5.9 · A capability claim is never refused because the open increments naming it in their touches wait: touches is a plan, never a lock (ADR-0944 D2). The waiting increment itself is still refused.

5.10 · A claim taken on branch `feature/signup` ends with a "merged" line once GitHub shows a pull request from that branch merged after the claim was taken, found at the next tool call or hook line; a pull request merged before the claim, or still open, ends nothing.

reported.note: 37 focused tests pass: no-merge board takes no project lock; observed merges still recheck current claims under lock and release them. Before/after benchmark includes both no-merge and actual-merge paths.

contracts.title: 5.11 · The public readings list current capability and increment claims and find the holder of one unit, with the same live or idle result on the terminal and the board. Released work and a unit in another project have no holder.

5.12 · Claude Code session A makes a workspace for a proposed increment: a new folder where its harness keeps worktrees, on a fresh branch cut from `origin`'s main as just fetched (a commit pushed after the clone is in it), and A holds the increment there, the claim naming that branch, and the increment is active. For Codex, preparation fetches main and returns its exact commit and a work-derived name for the app's `create_worktree`, without creating a folder, branch or claim. The agent then attaches the app's returned directory: Storytree verifies it is a linked worktree of this repository with HEAD at that exact commit, names a detached HEAD `codex/<name>` (keeps an existing named branch), and claims the work for that session on that branch. Moving `origin/main` after preparation does not change the expected commit.

5.13 · Making a workspace for work another live session holds, or for waiting work, is refused naming the holder or the blocker, and no folder, branch or claim is made, only a claim-refused line for held work (5.2); for work the session already holds it is refused naming the branch it holds it on. Codex checks before app creation and again when attaching; a claim lost to another session between the steps is refused naming that holder, leaving the app's worktree untouched.

5.14 · When main cannot be fetched fresh, as from a folder with no `origin`, it is refused saying why, and nothing is claimed or started. Attaching a directory from another repository, the main checkout, a subdirectory, or a worktree at the wrong commit is refused without claiming or changing it. If attaching fails after taking the claim (including naming a detached branch), that claim is released; the app's worktree is never removed (a started increment stays active).

5.15 · A claim cancelled while waiting for the activity lock or the increment activation write lock leaves no claimed line, activation or activation history. A capability or already-active increment claim checks cancellation before its claimed line too. Once admitted, a claim completes normally; a workspace claim creates or attaches its workspace only after admission.

5.16 · A claim's reason is its session's name in the running-sessions list, so it is held to 40 characters (measured from the list's label column at its default width): a claim, or a workspace, whose reason is longer is refused naming the limit and the reason's length, nothing is written and nothing is started; a reason of 40 characters or fewer is claimed as before (ADR-0737 D2).
5.17 · A holder last seen on this machine before it restarted is taken over at once

5.19 · Making a workspace for a capability from inside a worktree whose branch this session already holds work on claims the capability there, on that branch, and makes no second worktree or branch. Asking for a workspace for an available increment from inside any linked worktree (named or detached, from any subfolder, either harness) is refused with the command that claims it there, and no worktree, branch, preparation, claim or activation is made

5.23 · A claim takes from the library what deciding it needs and no more: one the session already holds takes almost nothing, and a capability claim takes about as much with five open increments naming it as with one.

reported.note: a claim already held under 32 KiB (was ~3 MB); five naming increments within 128 KiB of one; the edit-claims look reads the plan once

contracts.title: 5.25 · Making a workspace for work that already has an open pull request (a head branch named for it, `*/increment-<id>-*`) is refused naming each pull request and its branch, before anything is claimed or made, unless the session says to build beside it; a GitHub that cannot be asked refuses nothing
5.26 · The session manager ends a quiet session's claim with a release naming the holder and why; a live holder's claim is refused

5.27 · Closing or releasing an increment ends every capability claim taken while it was held, whoever closes it and whatever the disposition, in every reading; one claimed before it stands (ADR-0944 D5, ADR-0949 D4)
5.29 · Releasing an active increment without closing it, by the release tool, the session manager's release or close-out, returns it to proposal; a capability or a closed increment is untouched

5.31 · An edit tool aimed at a capability its session's claimed increment does not list, or that another live session holds by claim or on its increment's list, is refused before the edit, naming the way through or the holder; a file that declares no capability, or a session's own listed capability, is never refused (ADR-0949 D3)

5.33 · The session manager's worklist lists claimed increments whose holder is quiet, with no running command and no open pull request, routing a gone holder's to release and a quiet one's to ask; nothing is ended until the manager releases (ADR-0953 D4)
5.34 · A takeover's claimed line names the holder, how long it was quiet and why
5.35 · A refused claim names the increment its holder holds the work for

5.36 · A question one live session is putting to the owner is refused to another, naming it, and read as presented; it is free again once that session stops, ends or closes out, and a settled question is refused

5.37 · When a claim on an increment ends because its branch's pull request merged, that increment's pending plan changes are applied first, marked with the pull request and written by the session that saw the merge
5.38 · A refused capability claim names the increment its session holds it under
5.39 · A claim's mark is one shape and one colour wherever it is drawn

5.40 · An edit to a file in an imported folder is refused unless the session's increment lists the explored capability covering it; when it does, the user is asked (Claude Code) or the edit refused, never passed on the agent's own increment
5.41 · One user yes covers an increment's edits to imported code
5.42 · A yes said in the conversation counts for the session that heard it

5.43 · With `idle-after` set to 10m, a claim whose holder was last seen 15 minutes ago, with no command running, reads idle and can be taken over, and a session whose hooks report no turns reads waiting; unset (30 minutes), neither: a session whose hooks report its turns is never judged by it (ADR-0754 D5).
5.44 · A handed-over pull request keeps its session's claims until it merges or closes
5.45 · A fix session on the pull request's branch takes over its held claims
5.46 · Letting go of a pull request ends the claims held for it

5.47 · A worktree git makes while printing to stderr is made and claimed; one git fails to make is refused with git's own error line, never its progress line, and leaves no claim, folder or branch behind

5.48 · A session claiming again, from a linked worktree, work it holds on another branch holds it on that worktree's branch from then on; claiming it again from the main checkout leaves it where it is
5.49 · A red the watcher handles is a pr-red line on its pull request's holder
5.50 · A hand-over holds none of the claims taken on another branch
5.51 · A holder whose heartbeat stopped reads idle at once
5.52 · A renumbered file is placed by its session's increment's pending moves before the live plan, so a fold asks for no capability it never touches (ADR-0966)
5.53 · A capability on another live session's increment's list is refused at the claim, naming that increment and its holder
5.54 · A CI rerun the watcher starts is a ci-rerun line on the watcher, which reads as no session
5.55 · Several capabilities are claimed in one call, in ascending id order, all or nothing
5.56 · A hand-over also holds the session's branchless claims on the handed increment
5.57 · Clearing an owner wait to finish the work claims the increment first, through that wait
5.58 · Only an increment's live holder closes it; the owner's shell, the watcher, and anyone once it reads idle or unheld close it too
5.59 · A workspace for an increment claims every capability on its list, all or nothing, before the worktree is made

5.60 · The owners query names each file's capability and who holds it: another live session by its own claim or by an increment whose list names it, the caller itself, or nobody; a file with no capability names its story's package, and the free capabilities are offered to claim in one call
5.61 · Letting go of a merged pull request applies each held increment's pending plan changes, marked with it, before its claims end; an apply that fails ends none

capabilities.title: 9 · Context readings
capabilities.description:
How many tokens a session's own context window holds, worked out when it is asked for from what the hooks recorded (ADR-0725, ADR-0728; 0.2's `storytree context`, ADR-0716 O2). The hooks record each session's transcript path (capability 3). A reading is computed at ask time from that transcript as it stands, so it is fresh mid-turn, and in a `claude -p` run whose turn has not ended. On the session's own machine (the status line, `storytree context`) that means the transcript file itself. The app reads no transcript file: its readings and windows are parsed from the transcript records the hooks stream into the shared log (3.13; ADR-0749 D3), so an app on any machine reads every machine's sessions. Those records have obvious secrets scrubbed on the way in (9.12) and are kept 180 days, after which what was worked out from them is kept instead (9.13; ADR-0749 D4). A reading is a plain record: the session, its harness, tokens used, when it was read, and its source (the transcript it was read from). It carries no window size and no fraction (ADR-0728 D1). The guidance a session judges against is a token figure the user sets on the agent link settings surface (capability 10, `context-guidance`; ADR-0728 D2, D3). A reading states that guidance and whether tokens used are past it or under it (9.7); it is a soft line, never enforced. The same figure is the line past which a Claude Code session is nudged, through the prompt hook (capability 3), to hand off and start fresh (9.9; ADR-0739 D1): one setting, no second figure, and 0.2's separate 850,000 hard mark is not brought across. The nudge is advice; nothing stops the session. Codex sessions get no nudge until Codex matures (ADR-0739 D5). This capability owns the nudge because whether a session is past its guidance is this capability's reading (9.7); the prompt hook only carries the words. Built with advice once per session; later prompts in the same session do not repeat it.

For Claude Code, tokens used are the latest request of the session's own conversation: `input_tokens` + `cache_read_input_tokens` + `cache_creation_input_tokens`, counted once per `requestId`, with subagent (`isSidechain`) and `<synthetic>` lines left out. A transcript with nothing to count is an absence with its reason, never 0. For Codex, tokens used are the rollout's last token count. Any live session's reading can be worked out this way without that session asking, so the board can later show one per session; that display is not built here. It reads and never enforces: the session still decides whether to take on more work.

The transcript is always the one the hooks recorded as named by the harness (`transcript_path`, on every Claude Code and Codex hook input). Nothing ever looks for a session's transcript by folder. That is what fixes 0.2's two blind spots. 0.2 worked out who was asking from the `.claude/worktrees/<name>` folder the command ran in, then matched transcripts whose recorded `cwd` sat inside it. A batch (`claude -p`) session run from a main checkout or from outside that folder was refused or matched nothing (0.2 friction `storytree-context-cannot-read-a-batch-sessions-own-window`). A session that moved into a fresh worktree kept writing its transcript under the project directory of the folder it started in, so the new folder matched nothing. And because worktree folders are reused, the fallback could read another session's window (0.2 friction `context-verb-blinded-by-the-fresh-worktree-its-own-rule-mandates`: no reading from the new worktree, 506,097 tokens from the old one in the same minute).

As built (guidance-reading): `contextReading` and `readContext` add `guidance` without changing the existing session, harness, tokens, composition, at or transcript-source fields. Guidance is `{ value, source: "default" | "set", position: "under" | "at" | "past" }`, read afresh through capability 10's `readSettings`; its default is 600,000 tokens (ADR-0739 D1). An unusable settings file gives `{ absent: <the reader's reason> }` while retaining an available token count. No transcript remains an absence with no token count. `storytree context` and `read_context` state the guidance in their text and include it in their data; a count under, at or past guidance is never refused. Contract 9.7 is pinned in `packages/agent-link/src/context/context.test.ts`, and the existing 6.22 MCP test checks guidance output.

Remaining integration for 9.7: the current library-location routing reads the same settings file before it can open the activity log (ADR-0735). If that file is already unusable when `storytree context` or `read_context` starts routing, the call cannot reach the transcript record; the reader's token-preserving guidance error is therefore not reachable through those entry points in that case. This lane does not guess a local library or bypass the settings reader. Resolving that routing dependency is outside its context/tools-output file fence. Contract 9.7 must not be marked fully proved until that end-to-end case is resolved. `packages/agent-link/evidence/guidance-reading/captures.txt` records both the successful reader case and the route refusal.

As built (fresh-nudge): the Claude Code prompt hook calls the existing `readContext` for the session named by the recorded hook input. It adds advice to hand off and start a fresh session at the next safe boundary only when that reading is past its current guidance, naming both tokens used and the guidance. Definitions and context advice use separate per-session ledgers through the definitions hook's extracted `notYetGivenIds` helper; each nudge is given once per session across separate hook processes. Under or at guidance, absent readings, unreadable settings, and Codex inputs add no nudge. No threshold or switch is added: the existing reading supplies the sole setting, including the default change owned by capability 10. The built-hook contract 9.9 test covers boundaries, changed settings, repetition, definitions alongside advice, Codex, and absence/recovery; every prompt exits 0 with no blocking decision. The existing 9.7 routing qualification above remains.

contracts.title: 9.1 · A recorded Claude Code transcript whose last own request used 12,000 input, 300,000 cache-read and 5,000 cache-creation tokens reads 317,000 tokens used; a request repeated across lines with one `requestId` counts once, and a later subagent (`isSidechain`) or `<synthetic>` line does not change the figure.
9.2 · A transcript that is empty, unreadable, or holds only subagent or synthetic requests reads as an absence naming which, never as 0 tokens.
9.3 · A recorded Codex rollout reads its last token count as tokens used (ADR-0728: no window size).

9.5 · A session's reading is worked out when asked, from the transcript last recorded for it (3.12) read at that moment (9.1, 9.3), and carries the session, harness, tokens used, when it was read and its source; it carries a window size and fraction only when the session's Claude Code mod reported its usage (9.19, ADR-1056 D3 narrowing ADR-0728 D1). Any live session's reading can be worked out this way without that session asking. A session with no recorded transcript gives an absence, and another session's transcript is never read.

9.6 · `storytree context`, run with the harness's session id in its environment, prints that session's tokens used, worked out at that moment (9.5), even mid-turn with no turn ended since the transcript grew, and `--json` prints the record; it exits 0 whatever the figure, its sentence states no window size or fraction (its --json record carries the window and percentage when the session's mod reported them, 9.19), states the guidance as 9.7 says, and with no reading it says so and prints no number.

9.7 · A reading states the context guidance in effect (capability 10: set, or its default) and whether tokens used are past it or under it; with 400,000 set, 317,000 reads under and 450,000 reads past, and the command still exits 0. With the settings file unusable (10.4), the reading gives tokens used and says the guidance could not be read, and why.

9.8 · A Claude Code or Codex reading carries its composition: estimated tokens in four groups, sorted from the labels the harness put on each record, never from a body's words. Injected: the system prompt and tool list (the tokens of the first request, or Codex's first token count, less what the transcript recorded before it), Codex's base instructions and developer messages, project guidance, catalogues, hook output, reminders, file-change notices and harness-authored messages (for Codex, a user message it never recorded as the user's own). Grounding: what reading calls returned (file reads, searches, web and library reads, subagent digests, a shell command that only reads, such as a grep; a Codex exec cell whose every tool call only reads). Implementation: what changing calls returned (edits, writes, any other shell command, such as a test run; a Codex exec cell with any changing call, and a wait on it) and every call the session authored. Other: its own prose and reasoning, the human's words, and any label nothing sorts, named. Subagent lines and harness bookkeeping are left out; sizes are bytes at 3.8 characters per token, except an image (a screenshot read, a pasted picture), which counts at its pixels ÷ 750 tokens, at most about 4,800, as the model pays for it, never at its base64 length.

9.9 · A recorded Claude Code prompt hook input, for a session whose reading (9.5) is past the context guidance (9.7), makes the prompt hook add for the agent advice once per session to hand off and start a fresh session, naming its tokens used and the guidance; under or at the guidance it adds none. Later prompts in that session add no more advice, even if its reading crosses the guidance again; a fresh session may receive its own. It is advice: the hook still exits cleanly and the prompt is never refused. The same input from a Codex session past the guidance adds no advice (ADR-0739 D5), and with the guidance unreadable (10.4) or no reading, none is added.

9.10 · A session's window is read from its transcript (ADR-0746 D1, ADR-0756): the tool results it holds now (after the last compaction, with the segment Claude Code says it kept; never a subagent's side chain), each joined to the call that brought it by the id the harness wrote; each note or file it opened (the MCP server's open, a shell's storytree library read, a file-read tool, a shell cat, head, tail or sed -n), in order, with whether that read is still in the window; and the notes it only glimpsed: named in a result it holds now but never opened, each once, in the order first named. Claude Code transcripts and Codex rollouts both read; a harness storytree has no transcript reader for (Pi, Cursor) has no window, and says so, never one read as another's; nothing is inferred from timing or wording.

9.12 · Before a transcript record is stored, obvious secrets in it (API keys, bearer and OAuth tokens, private keys, connection-string passwords) are replaced by a marker naming what was removed ("[scrubbed: API key]", "[scrubbed: bearer token]", "[scrubbed: OAuth token]", "[scrubbed: private key]", "[scrubbed: password]"), and the record still parses; ordinary text passes untouched. The scrub is best-effort for obvious shapes, never a guarantee (ADR-0749 D4).

9.13 · The retention pass (the app runs it at each start) deletes raw transcript records older than 180 days; before they go, the session's context reading and window worked out from them are kept, and are what is read for that session from then on (ADR-0749 D4).

9.14 · A reading asked again over a session's stored transcript parses only the records stored since the last ask, and reads exactly as a reading of the whole transcript would (tokens, composition, guidance), for Claude Code transcripts and Codex rollouts alike, including a Codex user message whose UserMessage event arrives in a later ask; an ask with nothing new stored parses nothing. So the app's 10-second readings of long sessions cost what they gained, not their whole length (ADR-0836).

9.15 · storytree context reads the session STORYTREE_SESSION_ID names and refuses a shell naming none, saying how to name one; a transcript from a harness storytree does not know is never parsed as Claude Code's
9.16 · A Pi session's reading is its last own assistant message's total tokens, from the session file Pi writes
9.17 · A Claude Code subagent's reading comes from its own transcript, and its parent's is unchanged
9.18 · A project's sessions' spend adds every own request's input, cache and output once per request, a subagent's records, and Codex's running total, up to a time or only after one
9.19 · A reading takes its tokens, window and percentage from the session's latest reported usage, the transcript kept as the fallback when there is none or it carries no figure
9.20 · Each session's latest reported usage and latest failed turn are read together, for a lane's runner and the pool; a session with neither is left out
9.21 · Transcript records a cache keeps on disk are readable only by the user who runs it

capabilities.title: 12 · Record who started each run
capabilities.description:
Every tracked run names the session that started it and the computer where it runs. Background shells and detached servers keep that owner after the request or launcher that started them has gone away.

As built (foundation): @storytree/processes supplies one launchOwned boundary for resolved Claude Code/Codex callers and explicitly session-bound manual callers, with ownerFromCall accepting the agent link's public caller and agent context. Each launch durably records its owner, machine, optional project, executable/arguments, folder, launch time, PID and native lifetime observation before reporting tracked. Explicit parentRun/parentSession/subagent links survive the launcher; no PID adoption or folder/time/command inference assigns ownership. Failed launches or registration return a named gap, including a surviving PID when known. Installed CLI/MCP inventory, stop and clear doors are wired through the own package. Existing command hooks alone still do not register runs; this landing does not add launch coverage.

contracts.title: 12.1 · A registered run keeps its resolved session, machine, project when known, process identity, command, folder and start time.
12.2 · Two sessions in the same checkout keep separate process ownership, including when their command text is identical.
12.3 · A detached child registered at launch remains attributed after its launcher exits.
12.4 · A background command launched through the supported Claude Code, Codex or manual launch path has a durable ownership record before its launch is reported as tracked.
12.5 · A launch without a usable owner or successful registration reports that gap instead of assigning an owner by folder, start time or command text.

capabilities.title: 13 · Keep sight of unfinished runs
capabilities.description:
A request ending or timing out does not mean its work has stopped. Each run stays visible until the computer confirms it has ended, with anything it cannot establish shown as uncertain.

As built (foundation): readLedger and observeRuns retain records independently of requests, turns, sessions, claims and age, without a library connection. Request outcomes stay unknown unless the caller records evidence; explicit timeout evidence never implies process death. Native probes distinguish live/gone/unknown and compare Linux boot/start ticks, macOS boot/native microsecond start time or Windows exact creation FILETIME before attributing the current PID to a recorded lifetime. Failed or partial reads stay visible alongside readable records. Only registered runs and explicit child links are covered; unregistered launch paths and descendants remain untracked. Stopping and closing consume these observations in later capabilities and must revalidate identity before any signal.

contracts.title: 13.1 · A surviving process or owned child remains visible after a request timeout, labelling the request as timed out only when the caller supplied that evidence; otherwise its request outcome is unknown.
13.2 · Ending a turn, restarting or ending a session, releasing a claim, or passing twelve hours does not erase a surviving process record.
13.3 · A probe reports live, gone or unknown; unknown is never treated as confirmed dead.
13.4 · If a recorded PID has been reused, the replacement process is neither attributed to the old run nor signalled under its authority.
13.5 · Unreadable records and failed inventory reads remain visible as observation gaps alongside the records that could be read.

capabilities.title: 14 · See what remains
capabilities.description:
The session can list its remaining work or inspect all recorded sessions' work on this computer with an owner beside each run. The answer identifies what is running, what ended without reporting back, and what the inventory could not observe.

As built (listing API): @storytree/processes/listing exports listRuns and renderInventory over the foundation's observeRuns. The self view requires an explicit resolved owner and includes explicitly delegated descendants; the all-session view needs no owner and grants no cross-session stop authority. Rows keep command/arguments, folder, age, owner, machine, run/PID/lifetime identity and independent process/request findings. Only the inspector's exact lifetime is excluded. Read gaps, uncertain readings, foreign-machine records and coverage remain visible offline. Optional shared lifecycle readings have no stop action. The API offers an action only when a surface supplies an installed stop entry point and the row has an owned local live identity; otherwise it explains the absence.

As built (scope alignment): inventory uses the same ownership and conflicting-registration checks as stopOwned. An explicitly unknown calling agent refuses self inventory with a pointer to all-session inspection rather than reporting an empty scope. A named subagent sees only its own runs in self scope; its siblings and parent have no stop offer. Session callers retain explicitly delegated descendants, including established multi-hop parentSession links. An unchanged ledger no longer offers an action that stopping refuses for scope or conflicting ownership. Stopping still revalidates at invocation, so changed ownership or lifetime can alter the outcome.

As built (installed doors): storytree processes / own --all and MCP list_own_runs / list_all_runs call the listing API outside a project and with the app/database absent. Each self view offers only its installed stop entry point (CLI command or MCP tool), retaining the API's scope checks and explicit coverage. Both doors include the public app/database lifecycle reading as shared work with unknown native identity and no stop action, pointing to storytree app status / storytree app quit. An unknown shared lifetime keeps the overall reading incomplete.

As built (caller identity, supervisor-directed): with the app/database down, a CLI caller's self is the harness session named by CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID or CODEX_THREAD_ID, using the workspace command's environment seam. Missing or competing harness signals refuse self inventory, stop and clear and point to read-only own --all. MCP uses Codex's per-call session/thread metadata offline. When the library is reachable, exact call-id hook records supply the corrected session and named subagent, limiting it to its own runs. Claude MCP's shared server environment cannot identify an offline calling agent, so unresolved self operations refuse and point to list_all_runs / own --all. No authority is inferred from folder, timing, commands or a synthetic MCP session.

As built (delivery): the shared agent-link builder bundles both installed doors and stages Koffi's physical loader plus the host native module in its supported build/koffi/<ABI> prebuild layout, accepted by the unchanged installer payload verifier; the standalone CLI uses the same staging function. Desktop packaging replaces the host native package with the exact win32-x64 or win32-arm64 target before hashing each payload. The desktop manifest explicitly copies the native dependency directory as an extra resource, because electron-builder excludes a root node_modules directory from its general resource copy. Missing native targets fail the build. The habits card teaches all four own tools. Evidence: packages/processes/evidence/doors2/. Built CLI and stdio MCP tests execute native inventory/stop/clear on each CI host; Linux additionally assembled both Windows payloads and checked target PE architecture and manifest hashes. Real installed Windows x64/arm64 harness acceptance remains with the laptop supervisor.

contracts.title: 14.1 · The self inventory distinguishes live, unknown and gone runs with command, PID/run identity, age, owner and folder, excluding the inspecting command itself.
14.2 · The all-session view works without a current session identity and attributes every readable local run without granting cross-session stop authority.
14.3 · Self-scoped operations use the existing harness identity and refuse an unidentified caller rather than returning an apparently empty inventory.
14.4 · Inventory works while the app or database is unavailable and states its machine and launch coverage, including unsupported or unregistered paths.
14.5 · Live work is a normal inventory result, with a usable stop action for the caller's stoppable rows; shared or uncertain-identity rows explain why no such action is offered.
14.6 · The retained CLI forms and the MCP tools return the same ownership and process findings through the owning package's API.

capabilities.title: 15 · Stop the work I own
capabilities.description:
The session can stop the runs it names without stopping another session's work. It checks the run and its covered children after each attempt, and reports failure whenever their disappearance cannot be confirmed.

As built: `@storytree/processes/stopping` exports `stopOwned({ owner, targets, home?, graceMs?, forceMs? })`. Targets are registered run UUIDs. Parent sessions cover explicitly delegated sessions and registered `parentRun` descendants; a named subagent cannot stop its parent or siblings. Malformed/unregistered, foreign-machine and conflicting-owner targets are refused; uncertain or replaced lifetimes never authorize signalling.

Each result states its computer, registered membership, exclusions, gaps, attempts and final process readings. Ownership is reread before each delivery. Polite and forced phases each check the root and every covered child; survivors, unknown readings, ownership changes, late registrations and unreadable inventory make the result unsuccessful. All records remain for capability 5.

Coverage is explicitly `registered-runs-and-linked-descendants`, with `nativeTree: unconfirmed` and the foundation launch-coverage warning. A successful scoped stop is not proof that unregistered OS descendants or the whole computer are clear. Linux uses identity-checked pidfds; macOS uses combined birth/PID-version evidence and audit-token signals; Windows uses a FILETIME-checked handle, targeted WM_CLOSE when available, then bounded force. No process-group or PID-only fallback is used.

As built (installed stop doors): storytree processes stop <run…> and MCP stop_own_run call stopOwned directly. They preserve every per-target stopped, already-gone, refused or incomplete outcome, native-tree limits, exclusions and gaps; unsuccessful results exit nonzero / set MCP isError. Unknown callers receive no authority. CLI, bundled CLI, source MCP and bundled stdio MCP tests stop a real owned child while refusing another session or sibling. Online Claude hook attribution also retains the named subagent boundary after a session reset. Evidence: packages/processes/evidence/stopping/ and packages/processes/evidence/doors2/.

contracts.title: 15.1 · A stop outside the caller's explicitly established ownership/delegation scope is refused with its owner, while an unregistered or malformed target is refused without receiving a signal.
15.2 · A target whose original process is confirmed gone receives no signal; a reused PID or uncertain target identity cannot authorise a stop.
15.3 · Stopping an owned tree/group never includes a process with conflicting or unestablished ownership, and the covered membership is stated.
15.4 · A bounded initial stop and, under C1, forced escalation are each followed by checks of the root and covered children; a surviving child prevents a stopped result.
15.5 · A live or unconfirmed survivor keeps its record and makes the stop unsuccessful, regardless of whether the operating system accepted the signal.
15.6 · Multiple named targets each receive an outcome, and any refusal or survivor makes the overall result unsuccessful.

capabilities.title: 16 · Finish with an honest inventory
capabilities.description:
The session can clear records of work confirmed gone without hiding work that may still be running. Its closing check distinguishes an empty observed inventory from an incomplete observation, so a tidy record cannot become a false claim that the computer is idle.

As built: `@storytree/processes/closing` and `@storytree/processes` export `clearOwned({ owner, home?, knownGaps? })`, `readClosing({ home?, owner?, knownGaps?, shared? })` and `renderClosing(reading)`. Clear removes only the caller session/harness's records, with named subagents limited to their own records; delegated sessions' records are untouched. Original lifetimes and all registered descendants must be confirmed gone. Live, unknown and foreign records remain; unreadable records and known gaps prevent unproved child clearance. Removal failures are reported separately from successful removals.

Clear rereads records and child membership after probing and before unlinking. Changed, disappearing, reparented or newly registered children retain the affected parent; only this call's confirmed removals may shrink its previously observed membership. It preserves request evidence and gap records, never signals processes, and changes neither claims, sessions nor increments.

The closing reading reuses the listing API in all-session scope, irrespective of the caller, session end or released claims. Its status is `empty`, `remaining` or `incomplete`. Live/unknown rows stay visible; persisted read/registration gaps and caller-carried gaps whose persistence failed make it incomplete and name missing evidence separately. An empty verdict says “no tracked session work remains on this machine”, with the launch coverage and an explicit remote-machine limit. Shared work remains separately visible and is never stopped automatically.

These are point-in-time observations, without a launch interlock. Only explicitly registered descendants are covered; neither whole-machine idleness nor remote clearance is claimed. Evidence: `packages/processes/evidence/closing/README.md`, `red.txt`, `red-membership.txt`, `green.txt`, `gate.txt`, and the PR's three native CI checks. As built (installed clear doors): storytree processes clear and MCP clear_own_runs call clearOwned without signalling, preserve removed, retained, failed and gaps as separate fields, then return an all-session readClosing. Read gaps from clear are carried as knownGaps into that closing reading. Failed removals or clear gaps exit nonzero / set MCP isError while retaining the full result. Remaining live work and unknown shared app identity remain visible in the closing verdict; clear success does not claim closure or whole-computer idleness. The current doors perform no launches and have no additional unpersisted launch-gap source. Evidence: packages/processes/evidence/doors2/.

contracts.title: 16.1 · Clear removes only the caller's records whose original processes and covered children are confirmed gone, leaving every other session's records untouched.
16.2 · Clear retains live, unknown and unreadable records and reports failed removals rather than claiming they disappeared.
16.3 · The closing reading cannot say that no owned work remains while live or unknown work survives, even if the session has ended or its claims have been released.
16.4 · A known registration/read gap makes the closing reading incomplete under G1, with the missing evidence named separately from known live work.
16.5 · An empty closing reading says “no tracked session work remains on this machine” with its coverage, and never claims a whole-machine census or remote-machine clearance.

capabilities.title: 11 · Machines
capabilities.description: The computers that work on a project, each with a short name its owner gives it, its hostname and its id, read from what the trunks and machine.json already hold; a way to give this computer its name and to ask which one it is; and the sessions list showing each session's machine by that name.

contracts.title: 11.1 · `storytree machine name <name>` gives this computer a short name, kept with its hostname and id; a name another machine has, or one that is not a short name, is refused
11.2 · `storytree machine list` shows the project's machines, each with its name, hostname and id, and marks this one; `storytree machine this` says which one this computer is
11.3 · The sessions list shows each session's machine by its short name, or by its hostname while it has none
11.4 · An increment's machine is checked against Machines: a named machine is kept, "none" clears it, and any other name is refused naming the known ones

11.5 · On Linux, machine health reads the boot time, MemAvailable, the 15-minute load and the root disk, and names a concern for memory under its limit, load over it and a disk fuller than it, or a reading it could not take

11.6 · On Windows, machine health reads the boot time, the memory available, the processor queue and the system drive, and names a concern for each past its limit, or a queue PowerShell could not give
11.7 · `storytree machine health` reads the machine against the limits in settings: concerns come first and refuse, so the command exits 1, and a healthy machine answers with each reading

capabilities.title: 17 · Friction
capabilities.description: Every session files what fought it (friction) and the owner's redirections (re-steers), with evidence; a landing drains the open reports and routes each to its remedy with a reason. Its verbs (the friction and resteer families, and the record_friction, reinforce, record_resteer, friction_drain and route tools) are declared once here and mounted by both doors.

contracts.title: 17.1 · Friction with vague evidence is refused.
17.2 · A re-steer whose evidence is a paraphrase is refused.
17.3 · `reinforce` adds a dated recurrence, keeping the route of a routed report (a resolved or dismissed one reopens, ADR-1016 D2).

17.4 · It records friction with concrete evidence and a re-steer with the owner's quoted words, the agent's account kept apart; friction whose evidence is vague prose, a re-steer whose evidence quotes nobody, and a defect with no failure mode are each refused as a readable answer, and nothing is written. Shared capture stamps the calling branch and UTC date, and refuses a fourth friction report on that branch that day, counting routed reports too; the refusal names the cap and points to friction reinforce.

17.5 · Reinforcing friction through the tool or public capture function appends dated concrete evidence to the same item and preserves the route of a routed one (a resolved or dismissed one reopens, ADR-1016 D2). Invalid recurrences write nothing.

17.6 · The daily friction cap counts each writer's own reports: on a branch every session shares, a second session's report is accepted after another filed three that day, and each is still refused its own fourth; a report whose writer was not recorded counts toward every writer's three

17.7 · A re-steer whose evidence is the user's exact words without quotation marks is refused naming the step that passes, putting those words inside double quotation marks, and the same words inside them are then recorded

17.8 · The friction drain holds at most three open friction reports (ADR-1016 D1) that another session filed, never one filed from the session's own branch. Reports with the most recurrences come first, with oldest first on ties; no recurrences counts as zero, and missing provenance still counts as another session's report.

17.9 · route(friction, route, reason, options?) records the routing judgement with its reason and an optional dischargedBy reference to the remedy that landed. The reference is trimmed and must be non-empty when supplied; omitting it preserves an existing stamp. An already-routed report can receive its stamp later. A route with no reason or a blank delivery reference is refused without writing.

17.10 · A tool route requires a live, non-closed increment whose remedies names this friction, unless the report already carries a delivered-by stamp or receives one in this call. An unrelated or closed increment is insufficient; refusal writes nothing and explains the missing remedy or delivery reference.

17.11 · A report already routed is routed again only to the same route (a later delivery stamp or a clearer reason); routing it elsewhere is refused naming the earlier route and its reason, and nothing is written, so two librarian passes cannot silently replace each other's judgement.

17.12 · Every route but nothing needs a live, non-closed increment whose remedies names the report, or a delivery stamp given now or already carried; refused otherwise with nothing written. The drain lists open reports, so one reopened is offered again and may be routed afresh

17.13 · The friction drain leases the reports it lists to the session that asked, for a few minutes; a second session draining in that window is handed the next unleased reports, not the same ones, and a lease ends when the report is routed or the lease lapses
17.14 · route() checks whether a report is already routed inside its write, not before it, so two passes racing to route one report two ways write one route and refuse the other

17.15 · `friction route <friction> --to <route> --reason …` records the route and reason, with an optional --discharged-by stamp; its refusals (a tool route with no live remedy) reach the caller unchanged and write nothing (ADR-0789 D2).
17.16 · `friction drain` lists the friction drain for the calling branch: up to three unrouted reports other branches filed, most recurrences first (ADR-0789 D2).
17.17 · Session management declares the `friction` and `resteer` families the command line lists 13th and 14th: friction filed on one branch, with its links and the writer, is drained on another

17.18 · Session management declares its friction tools once, and the MCP server serves them from its declarations: record_friction, reinforce, record_resteer, friction_drain and route; a capture refusal answers as a refusal with nothing written

capabilities.title: 18 · Scheduled processes
capabilities.description: The runner's two commands: which scheduled process records are due now, and recording that one ran with its outcome, so a factory's routines are run when their schedule comes round.

contracts.title: 18.1 · A scheduled process is due once its schedule comes round after its latest run, unless its time is past its grace or its precheck finds nothing to do
18.2 · A recorded run stops a process being due, and its outcome reads back; missed and skipped are recorded only when still so
18.3 · A plugin librarian's run is listed due on its trigger

capabilities.title: 19 · Worktree setup
capabilities.description: Right after storytree makes a worktree in a user's project, or a Codex session attaches the one its app just made, it runs the setup the project's own untracked local file names (.storytree/worktree.local.json): setup commands, gitignored files copied from the main checkout, and folders shared from it, so the agent never starts in an empty checkout. A team's checked-in .storytree/worktree.json, with the same keys, is read beside it, the local file winning key by key; its setup and teardown commands run only once the user has approved that exact set at their own terminal (`storytree workspace approve-setup <fingerprint>`, kept per repository in their settings), are asked again when they change, and are skipped with a reason, never blocking the worktree, when an agent runs alone. The file's teardown commands run, in a process of their own, when the reaper is about to remove a worktree set up this way.

contracts.title: 19.1 · A workspace made in a project whose untracked `.storytree/worktree.local.json` names setup commands, files to copy and folders to share runs each command in the new worktree, copies each file or folder from the main checkout and shares each folder (a junction on Windows), and its answer reports each step

19.2 · A setup step that fails (a command exiting non-zero, a path with `..`, an absolute path or a link leading out of the repository, a path git does not ignore, a missing source, a copy over the cap, or a local file git tracks or cannot parse) is reported naming why, the rest still run, and the claim and the worktree are kept
19.3 · A workspace made in a project with no `.storytree/worktree.local.json` is made exactly as before: nothing is run, copied or shared, and its answer reports no setup

19.4 · A worktree set up from the local file that names teardown commands has them run in it, in order, by a process of their own once the reaper would remove it, and is removed on a later pass once they have finished, a failed one included; a worktree never set up runs none

19.5 · A Codex session attaching the worktree its app just made at the prepared commit has it set up from the local file, reported in the attach's answer, and set up once however often it attaches; a Claude Code session attaching its own worktree runs no setup

19.6 · A checked-in `.storytree/worktree.json` is read beside the local file, the local file winning key by key, and its setup and teardown commands run only once the user has approved that exact set: before then, or after they change, the workspace is made without them and its answer names the command that approves them

19.7 · `storytree workspace approve-setup <fingerprint>` records the user's approval of the checked-in setup's commands only from a person at their own terminal, and is refused, recording nothing, when the fingerprint is not the checked-in file's current one

19.8 · When an agent runs alone (its harness says no one is attending), an unapproved checked-in setup's commands are skipped and the workspace's answer says no one is here to approve them, rather than asking

stories.title: Desktop app
stories.description: Storytree's desktop window: it starts the local library, lists the projects on the computer, mounts each story's surface and keeps itself up to date. Owns packages/app and apps/desktop.

depth.reason: flags: additive schema, credentials, record writes, release path, screen

radius.reason: 1 package downstream; serves invited users itself

guardrails.check: A model starts the real app (or the built website) from seeded fixtures at the state nearest the change and clicks through only that part, pass or fail with pictures (2.12). The real app: build it (`pnpm --filter @storytree/desktop build`), then from the checkout's root run `node --import tsx apps/desktop/check-app-linux.mjs`, under a display (on Linux `xvfb-run -a`; on the Mint box, which has no xvfb-run and whose display :0 is only usable while someone is logged in at it, append `--ozone-platform=headless` to the command instead (it runs the real app with no display); on the Windows laptop it runs as is), with STORYTREE_SMOKE_SCREENSHOT set to a path to keep its picture: it seeds a throwaway library and starts the app on it. Never `pnpm smoke` or `pnpm desktop:smoke`: they start the app on the live library. The page alone: the capture kit in apps/desktop/src/capture (its README). The website: `pnpm --filter @storytree/website build`, then open the built pages in Chromium.

capabilities.title: 1 · Lifecycle
capabilities.description: When the app opens it starts the database that holds every project's library, and it keeps it running until the app is quit: closing the window leaves both running in the background, with a tray icon whose Quit stops them, so agents' work is still recorded. The app can also be controlled from outside (ADR-0656 D0): asking it to quit from the command line stops it as the tray's Quit does. There is one owner at a time: opening the app again brings its window forward, another program holding the database is named, and while it runs the app leaves records saying where the database is and how to open the app, which is how an agent's session finds it or opens it.

contracts.title: 1.6 · With storytree closed, an agent's session start opens it: the installed app where there is one, never a development copy in its place.

1.7 · Closing the window leaves the app and its database running; the tray's Quit, or asking the app to quit from outside (`storytree app quit`), stops them: it stops the database once, and the app exits only after it has stopped. Quitting, including smoke teardown and restarting into an update, stops the page's polling before closing the library, without logging a closed-library error.

1.8 · Each project gets a snapshot in `~/.storytree/0.3/backups/<project>/` once a day, keeping that project's newest 14 (ADR-0641 B1): when the app starts it takes one of each project whose newest successful snapshot is missing or a day old and reuses one under a day old, and while it runs it takes the next at each project's day mark; a failed or partial snapshot does not count. A snapshot is one JSON object written a line per record and history entry, never built as one string, so a project past JavaScript's longest string (about 512 MB) is still backed up, and `readBackup` reads a file back line by line as the object `restore` takes. On POSIX, backup directories are private (0700) and partial and published snapshots are owner-readable and writable only (0600), independent of umask or an existing traversable application home. Startup and direct backups repair retained snapshot and partial permissions, including those of removed projects, before reuse; unrelated files keep their contents and modes. On Windows, backup directories and retained snapshots have protected DACLs granting only the current user access, and each partial is created exclusively with that DACL before snapshot bytes are written. Retained permissions are repaired before freshness reuse; a permission failure writes no new snapshot and prevents reuse. Unrelated home files and unrelated children keep their permissions and contents. Effective-access tests on Windows exclude an unrelated non-administrative identity even under permissive inherited and explicit ACLs; privileged administrator override is outside this promise.
1.9 · With the library set to Cloud SQL, the app starts no local Postgres and opens its projects, surfaces and snapshots on the instance; quitting leaves the instance alone.

1.10 · With the library set to Cloud SQL and the instance unreachable (no Google sign-in, a refused account, or no answer in time), the window says so in the refusal's own words and what to fix, and the app never falls back to the local library.

1.11 · With the library on Cloud SQL, where the app starts no local database, the running app is still found (its launch record carries its process id): storytree app quit quits it, a stopped app reads as not running, and a delivery waits for the app itself rather than for a database it never starts.

1.12 · The installed app opens at sign-in, straight to the tray with no window, unless the user has turned that off in the gear's Updates section; a development copy or a portable build never registers itself

reported.note: apps/desktop/src/main/sign-in.test.ts, merged in #372

contracts.title: 1.13 · A start that fails ends the app instead of lingering half-started
1.14 · The window keeps drawing through the machine's GPU resets: repeated GPU process crashes never block the app from WebGL, so a lost globe is restored instead of staying white until a restart
1.15 · Started with --callback-check, the app reports each sign-in callback a later start hands it, and whether it reached the sign-in session, without opening a window or its library
1.16 · A page operation a story declares reaches that story's answer in the main process, with the page's arguments

1.17 · The tray, the window and the packaged app wear the mark: the tray and window in the night colourway on a dark taskbar and the day colourway otherwise, following a change while running; the installer and app bundle in the day colourway

1.18 · A story's page operations its package's manifest names are answered in the main process and offered to the page, with neither main.ts nor bridge.ts naming the story to mount it (the page's type may still name its bridge, ADR-1030 D3)
1.19 · The page's errors reach app.log

1.20 · The desktop app answers no page operation of a story part switched off on this computer: each of its channels refuses, saying the part is off and how to switch it on, and every other part's operations are answered
1.21 · A page title change reaching a destroyed window is ignored, never an uncaught error; a live window gets the title with the build
1.22 · The main process's uncaught errors reach app.log
1.23 · After a logged main-process error, the app offers Keep going or Restart
1.24 · A factory plugin standing in for a switched-off part answers its page operations and serves its views in the part's place
1.25 · Each uncaught main-process exception and unhandled rejection is one record in the user's own library; a repeat adds to its count
1.26 · When the library cannot take a main-process error, app.log keeps it and nothing more is raised
1.27 · A second start, the dock's activate or the tray brings the window back, opening it again if it was closed; none reaches a destroyed window, and none opens one while the app is quitting
1.28 · The window's page never navigates away or opens another window, and the window shows itself once ready unless the app runs headless; a window destroyed first is left alone
1.29 · The page's reads and project choice, asked before the library opens, get no projects or are refused saying it is not open; once it opens, or reopens, each is answered by the library open then

1.30 · Started with --smoke, the app exits red on any main-process error, one raised while it quits included, after closing, reopening and quitting its window at awkward moments, and never waits on an error box

1.31 · While the user's library holds an app error not yet marked submitted, the app asks on opening to have their agent submit a GitHub issue, and stops asking once it is marked submitted from that box

1.32 · After five restarts in a row the app stops restarting itself, on every channel, keeps running its build, and records the stop as an error the user is asked to report; a start that stays up 30 minutes resets the count
1.33 · A start writes each timing mark once to app.log, as milliseconds from launch
1.34 · Everything the app says is kept in app.log in its home, which stays bounded
1.35 · The window's session grants only writing plain text to the clipboard, and refuses every other web permission request and check

1.36 · Started with --smoke, the app prints a smoke: line as each phase starts, keeps Electron's files in a scratch folder of its own so an open app's folder cannot hold it, and a run that gives up names the phase it was stuck in

1.37 · The desktop app composes the project records its story packages' manifests name (the QA ledger's), bundled and unbundled, and the setup help's Delete forgets them with a project, but a switched-off part's
1.38 · A main-side failure reaches the page in its own words
1.39 · The app takes its flags only from a start with no sign-in link, before '--', its developer flags only in development or CI, and no network or device path for a screenshot
1.40 · An unreachable library is said once per outage, not a stack per poll
1.41 · The page and its files are served from the app's own scheme, never file://, and a page-check start proves the page loads and its road worker answers
1.42 · The app opens its projects with the kinds of record its mounted factory plugins declare
1.43 · Quitting stops the journey, then the page reads, then the library, then Postgres, once however often it is asked; a part that fails to stop is said and the next stops all the same
1.44 · The app restarts itself only while it is not stopping, asked again after the seed check, no seed is being written to its own Postgres, and no backup holds it
1.45 · A library whose data folder another program holds is said as in use by that program, or another program, with its process and what to do; any other failure says why it could not be opened

1.46 · The main process bundles into one file for Electron that loads nothing from outside it but Node's own modules, Electron and the optional modules it never loads or loads lazily, so a packaged app needs no node_modules
1.47 · The preload script, bundled as the app bundles it, gives the page the bridge as `storytree` and nothing else, with the main process's answers on sign-in for feedback and stand-ins

capabilities.title: 2 · Storytree projects
capabilities.description: The app lists the storytree projects in its database and shows one at a time. Its always-visible, full-width top app bar holds only a gear at the right. The gear opens a large centred overlay with Projects, Settings, Updates and Help sections. Projects moves the whole app to another project in place; Settings mounts the agent link's per-user panel, Updates mounts the app's existing update status, and Help mounts app-setup's existing help surface. capabilities.title: 4 · Updates
capabilities.description:
The app keeps itself up to date by itself: on the owner's machine it runs from its own copy of merged main, notices new merges within a few minutes, and rebuilds and restarts itself in the background, so it never runs unmerged work and nobody rebuilds it by hand. Check for updates in the top-right gear asks that same merged-main updater to check now and shows the running build and its progress or failure. A ready build waits with the window open until no seed or start-up or daily snapshot is being written. A checkout explains that it does not update itself. Installed apps select releases from their own channel: development follows each merged release; stable follows only the owner-pinned existing build (ADR-0871). As built (increment_aca4e6853237): an installed app's downloaded release waits for a quiet moment (packages/app whenToInstall: ten minutes after launch, ten minutes without window input or agent activity from a session that has not ended), because a first install was replaced 17 seconds after setup said the app was open (packages/app-setup/evidence/acceptance, F1). The gear answers from the release updater in an installed app, marks itself with a dot while an update is pending, and its Restart to update installs at once. A seed or snapshot still holds any restart, including one requested from the gear. The owner accepted contracts 4.4 and 4.7's wording for this on 2026-09-29 (question_df551985ad62).

As built (increment_c3e1441890f9, contract 4.12): installed release updates read named, independent run holds under the app home/update-holds before each automatic installation. packages/app/src/updates/hold-run.mjs wraps a foreground command, publishes its hold before launch, removes it on return and preserves its exit code. Holds expire after the requested positive duration, at most six hours; overlapping runs do not release one another. Downloads continue, the pending status names the run, and the user's Restart to update still overrides holds while respecting seed writes and snapshots. The standalone wrapper and usage/proof are in packages/app/evidence/update-hold. No laptop acceptance run is part of this implementation.


As built (increment_402e76453e34, contract 4.17): the follow-main updater start-checks each new build before it may restart into it (apps/desktop/src/main/start-check.ts, wrapping follow-main's build through mainUpdates' update option). The build is started with --start-check, which goes only as far as registering the main process's handlers and exits 0: no library, no network, so a library on Cloud SQL or a local Postgres the running app holds never holds back a good build. A check that does not exit 0 within 60 s fails the build as 4.2 does, and that commit is remembered and not rebuilt. Lifecycle 1.13: run()'s rejection now ends the app (exit 1) instead of leaving it half-started holding the single-instance lock.

As built (increment_78ac958384c9, contracts 4.4 and 4.13): the follow-main updater restarts into a built main commit only at the moment the user's install choice allows, as a downloaded release does. Owner, 2026-10-21: the follow-main app "keeps closing on me" (app.log held 1,135 restarts). mainUpdates takes a quiet option; the desktop builds one quietMoment check (packages/app/src/updates/install-moment.ts: whenToInstall over launch time, window use, agent activity and the saved install choice) and gives it to both updaters. A built commit waiting for that moment reads pending, so the gear offers Restart to update, which restarts at once in every mode; seeds and snapshots still hold either restart. Settings → Updates offers When updates install in an app following main as well, and a pending update says when it installs: at the next quiet moment, during quiet hours, or when you click Restart to update. With agents working on the laptop most of the day, quiet mode may rarely find a moment; quiet hours is the predictable choice.
