stories.title: Work board
stories.description: A read-only drawer over the map view showing the project's arcs and increments (what landed, what is in progress, what waits) and the questions waiting on the owner. Owns packages/arc-surface.

radius.reason: 7 packages downstream; public users, inherited from packages/website

capabilities.title: 1 · Work states
capabilities.description: Every part, increment and arc shows exactly one state, worked out by one rule from the records, so no two views, and no two lines of one view, can disagree. A part is planned, in progress or landed; an increment, once closed, is landed or not completed (failed, withdrawn, or closed with nothing recorded), and before that is waiting on you, queued, held by an agent or open; an arc is waiting, blocked, claimed, idle, quiet, parked or closed.

contracts.title: 1.1 · A part no line names is planned. A claim makes it in progress, a landed report makes it landed, and a new claim after landing makes it in progress again.
1.2 · A part that is released, or whose window closes, without landing stays in progress, with nobody on it.
1.3 · A story is planned while every part is planned or it has no parts, landed once every part has landed, and in progress otherwise.

1.4 · A closed increment reads landed only when a landing was recorded or it carries a pull request. Every other close, whether failed, withdrawn or closed with nothing recorded, reads not completed (red), with the hover naming which. Nothing reads landed merely because it closed.

An open increment gets one reading, first match wins: waiting on you (held on a question you have not settled, or by a wait for an action of yours with its note while it waits on no open work; it drops back the moment you settle or clear it), then queued (its own wait, or its arc's, still holds, or a wait for an outside event before its check-back day, or a wait for an action of yours on work that still waits on open work, until that work lands), then held (an agent holds it, idle or not), then blocked (unclaimed, and its capabilities list names a capability another open increment holds through a live session; it names that increment and clears when it closes or releases, ADR-0949 D3), then open. An event wait past its check-back day holds nothing, and the reading says check-back passed (ADR-0938 D1). A proposal is never by itself waiting on you, but a question you have not settled holds it as it holds any open increment (ADR-0909 D2). An active increment whose agent released it reads open, still in progress, with nobody on it.

reported.note: Dropped the proposal exclusion in incrementState; the library's heldOn reading already carries proposals' holds (work-in-flight.ts:661).

contracts.title: An arc reads one state, first match wins: closed or parked, as recorded; then waiting (a question on it you have not settled); then blocked (its own wait still holds); then queued (every open increment is held, on a wait, on you or blocked by another increment, and it names what it waits on); then in progress (a live session holds one of its open increments, ADR-0949 D1); then ready · N to take (N open increments nobody holds and nothing holds up), even while an idle agent holds other work on it: an idle claim does not hide free work (ADR-0938 D3); then idle, shown "in progress · idle N min" (every agent on it is idle and nothing is free); then quiet (nothing open). Queued, ready and quiet are read from its increments on every live reading (ADR-0760 D1).

capabilities.title: 2 · Agents on the board
capabilities.description: Every increment and part an agent holds shows which agent: Claude Code or Codex, when its window opened, the reason it gave when it claimed, and whether it is live or idle, and for how long. It reads the agent link's own claim reading, so the overlay and the claim tool always agree, and an idle holder still holds its work.

contracts.title: 2.1 · An increment Claude Code holds shows "Claude Code", when that window opened, and its reason. Two Claude Code windows are told apart by when they opened.
2.2 · After 30 quiet minutes the holder reads "idle for N min" and still holds the increment. Once it releases or lands it, its window closes, or its pull request merges, nobody is on it.
2.3 · A Codex holder whose hooks never ran is flagged "hooks not running".

2.4 · An arc's holders come only from its open increments: the agent holding one of them, or a capability claimed under one of them (ADR-0949 D1). A capability claim counts toward the increment it was taken under, never an arc directly; a closed increment contributes nothing, so a capability held by another arc's session reads nothing on an arc whose landed increment lists it.

capabilities.title: 3 · Arc surface
capabilities.description: A full-width arcs-only bar sits below the app story's separate gear-only app bar and opens one read-only drawer over the forest. The bar carries no project name. Both bars reserve their space above the forest so its controls remain reachable, and the drawer opens below them. The drawer, half the window's height, leaves the forest usable below; it can be expanded to fill the window below the bars and restored (3.10). It lists root arcs as dense two-line lanes (state chip, title and small counted wait marks, then the bars alone, wrapping), with a bar for each increment, finished work first, each bar coloured by its work state, a count of what landed and what is open spoken on the bars' label but not shown (ADR-0980), and a chip with the lane's state and who is on it; Active, Parked and Closed each show their own arcs. It stays current while it is open: about every two seconds it asks for what changed in the library and the agent log, which the app carries to it, and it re-checks the clock once a minute, so an agent that goes quiet turns idle without any new record.

contracts.title: 3.1 · A full-width 48 px bar labeled Arcs sits directly below the app's separate 48 px gear-only bar, spans the whole window and carries no project name. Clicking either end opens or closes the drawer below both bars; the bar also works from the keyboard and Escape closes it, returning focus to the bar. The forest and its controls remain below both bars and receive input below the closed bar or the half-height open drawer while the app overlay is closed; an expanded drawer (3.10) covers them until it is restored or closed. The gear remains reachable above the arc bar and open drawer at wide and narrow window sizes. No action writes library data, and it carries no Library switch or artifact links. While its first read is on the way it says so, and a read that fails says so rather than drawing an empty board.

3.2 · Each root lane has its state chip, its title and its wait marks on line one, then its increments alone on line two: one fixed-size flat oval per increment in its state colour, finished ones first and then open ones, longest-waiting first, wrapping onto further lines when they do not fit; a claimed increment's oval carries its holder's flag (the globe's pennant in the session's colour, furled and greyed while the holder is idle), and the ovals sit close under the title, leaving only a flag's headroom (ADR-1003). The count ("3 landed · 1 not completed · 2 open", skipping zeros, never a percentage) is not shown; it is the ovals' accessible label (ADR-0980).

3.3 · Lanes sort by their arc's priority first, 1 first and unranked last, and a ranked lane shows it as "P1" beside its chip (ADR-0963). Within one priority they sort waiting, blocked, in progress, idle, ready, quiet, then the most recently active; a ready lane that also has idle claims sorts with the ready lanes. An arc tag never says claimed: a live holder reads "in progress" and an idle chip carries its age on its face ("in progress · idle 42 min", ADR-0949 D1), and its hover names who holds what; a ready lane that also has idle claims names them, with their age and the work held, in its chip's hover. At the right of its title a lane counts what its open increments wait on: an hourglass with the number of distinct other work and event note waits that still hold, and a question mark with the number of its open questions and owner note waits that still hold; a mark with nothing to count is not drawn, and each mark's hover and accessible label carry the full wording. Each bar's hover names its note waits (ADR-0938 D2, ADR-0980). Active shows on the first launch, then the saved scope is restored; Parked and Closed show only their own arcs, and there is no "All".
3.4 · In the app: a claim written while the overlay is open shows on it within about two seconds, without reopening.
3.5 · In the app: with no new line, a holder turns idle once the quiet time passes. The test uses a stand-in clock.

3.6 · In the app: the smoke check visits every scope and opens every root queue caret, then judges document.body.dataset.drew.arcSurface against the expected root lanes, expanded queue chips, root-lane increment bars and their agent marks. It does not count +N descendants or queued increments as drawn bars.

3.7 · Between launches, each project remembers drawer open/closed, scope and selected arc. A valid saved arc is restored; if it disappears the normal briefing fallback applies. Closing keeps scope and selection for the next open.
3.8 · The app's Surfaces menu lists the arc surface as Arcs, with no settings, on until the user switches it off; switched off, it is saved and reads off at the next launch (ADR-0750)

The open board re-reads the work only when its news holds an arc, increment or question change: news of lines alone, or of other records, redraws it from the work it already has, with the new lines. It reads the work itself at once when it opens and draws fresh when that lands, without waiting on the page reading's first read; news the page already held then is not read again, and a drawer reopened on the same page draws its last board ready, not refreshing. Each reading carries the library's waits for the owner or an event (waitsFor) with the holds; an absent one reads as none.
3.10 · The open drawer expands to fill the window below the two bars and restores to half height, the choice kept per project

3.11 · The arc surface declares the `arc` family, with `arc increment` within it, and the `question` family, that the command line lists 2nd and 3rd: a question raised holding an increment on its arc holds it, an empty --held-on clears the hold, and retiring a record that is no question names library retire

3.12 · The board reads live arcs and those closed yesterday and today; the Closed tab's Today and Yesterday draw from that, and 7 days or a From–to asks the library for its window when it changes, the kept board holding only the routine read

3.13 · `arc status` gives one line per active arc, moving ones first, each with its state and why: Working (increment, session, machine, since), Landed since --since (with its pull request), Ready, Waiting on you (question titles or owner-wait notes), Blocked (on what, until when) or Idle (nothing parked); the strongest state printed, the other mentioned

3.14 · `arc status` reads the board's arcs and the holds once each however many arcs there are, counts landings from the last two hours unless --since names a time or a span (30m, 2h, 1d), and refuses any other --since
3.15 · `arc recent` lists what landed since --since grouped by arc, each landing with its title and its pull request, then the arcs that closed since then; withdrawn, open and older work is left out
3.16 · `arc recent` reads the board's arcs once, counts from the last 24 hours unless --since names a time or a span (30m, 2h, 1d), and refuses any other --since

3.17 · `arc increment edit --escape-of <pr|increment> --escape-story <story>` records the escape an increment fixes, `--escape-of none` clears it, and one flag without the other is refused with nothing written
3.18 · The mounted drawer says once when it first draws a freshly read board
3.19 · Once the project has a repository cut-over, arc recent and arc show say a pull request closed before it as the old repository's owner/name#n, and one closed on or after it as #n
3.20 · The picked arc's title stays selected across a drawer refresh that changes nothing, and a copy button beside it puts the title on the clipboard as plain text, saying Copied

capabilities.title: 4 · Waits
capabilities.description: Every arc or increment that waits on other work says so and names what it waits for: an arc queued behind another arc folds away under that arc’s lane, behind a ▸/▾ caret in a fixed gutter; expansion shows chips, and an increment waiting on another increment, on any arc, draws yellow and names its blocker and why. A blocker shows what it holds up, a wait that will never release by itself says so, and an arc with something waiting on you is never hidden under its blocker.

contracts.title: 4.1 · An arc waiting on an open arc, or whose every open increment waits on work in another open arc, appears only as a chip under that arc's initially collapsed caret, not also at the top; waiting on several, it sits under the first on the board. Selecting the chip opens the queued arc's briefing. Once the wait releases, or it has work nothing holds up, it returns to the top, with nothing written. Waits that form a loop are cut at the loop's first arc on the board, so no arc disappears (ADR-0760 D1).

4.2 · A one-behind-one queue draws as a chain (A → B → C). Two arcs behind one blocker draw as a set, with a · separator and no arrow between them. A queued arc that holds up others carries "+N", one also waiting on another arc says "+1 other wait", and one queued by its increments names the increment it waits on in the arc above it.
4.3 · An arc with a question waiting on you stays at the top while it waits on another arc, and its other open bars still read queued.

4.4 · An increment waiting on another names it, its arc and the reason, and the blocker names what it holds up. If the blocker closed without landing, or cannot be found, the wait says it will not release by itself.

capabilities.title: 5 · Briefing
capabilities.description: Picking a lane, or a queued arc, opens its briefing: rows you scan, each a door into its prose, and no prose until something is opened (ADR-0980 D5). The arc's intent is one folded line. Its questions are one table, open first, each row a title and a status (open or settled); opening a row replaces the table with the full reading, the answer on top when settled, and “← back to questions” restores it. The reading is statement first, with its stakes, diagram, options as for and against, a recommendation marked not binding, and the longer parts folded with their word counts. After the questions, every increment on the arc is a row: its colour, its title and one short cell of chips for what it is doing, landed ones folded behind one row; opening a row shows its objective, its waits by name, the questions it waits behind, what it holds up, who holds it and how it closed.

contracts.title: 5.1 · Picking an arc shows its title, its intent folded behind one closed line, then its questions as one table, open first, each row its title and its status (open or settled); an arc with no questions shows no questions section. The drawer restores a valid saved selection; otherwise it opens on the first arc with a question waiting on you (or the first lane).

5.2 · Opening a question row swaps the panel for one full reading; “← back to questions” restores it. The full reading is statement first, then stakes, the diagram or "no diagram stored", options split into for and against, the recommendation marked not binding, and analogy and context folded with their word counts. The row itself shows no word count, no diagram note and none of the question's prose.

5.3 · A settled question stays in the one table, below the open ones, with its status "settled"; it stops counting as waiting, and its answer shows only when it is opened, on top of its reading. A settled question published with only its title and answer opens on those two alone, with no empty headings.

5.4 · A parked arc's briefing says once, on its questions, that the open ones are parked with the arc (they wait for it to be unparked), never "Waiting on you", and a parked arc's question does not pick the drawer's first briefing

5.5 · After the questions, every increment on the arc is one row: its bar's colour, its title on one line and one short cell of chips, never a sentence: "you" when it waits on the owner (a held question, an owner note, or questions behind its waits), "N increment(s)" for waits on other work, "event", "check-back passed", "blocked" by another increment's claim, the holder's label with its quiet minutes, "to take", "not completed", or a landed one's pull request number. Open work comes first (waiting, in progress, to take), then not completed, then landed, folded behind one "N landed" row.

5.6 · Opening an increment row shows in place its objective, each wait by name with its reason (the name alone when it has none), the owner's questions it waits behind, what it holds up, who holds it and how it closed (disposition, pull request, note), never its planning body; the intent fold, the landed fold and opened rows stay open across the live redraw.

stories.title: The command line
stories.description: `storytree` is the command a person types in a terminal to read and change their project's records. It is a front door and nothing more: each command is handed to the function its owning story already has (the library, Session management), so the command line and the agent's tools can never disagree.

radius.reason: 0 packages downstream; no audience of its own or downstream, so owner

capabilities.title: 1 · Front door
capabilities.description: `storytree <family> <verb>` works out which project the folder you are in belongs to, opens that project's library, and hands the command to the owning story's function, keeping no rule of its own. Every answer is a short plain sentence or listing; where it names records it may offer, under `next:`, the commands that open them, and nothing else (ADR-0786). A failure exits non-zero and says what to do; a command it does not have answers with the real one for that job.

contracts.title: 1.1 · In a project folder, `storytree library search <word>` finds an artifact written through the library.
1.2 · In a folder that is not a project, it exits non-zero with "not a storytree project".
1.3 · With storytree stopped, it says "storytree isn't running" within a second.
1.4 · A record the library refuses reaches you as the library's own message, and nothing is written.
1.5 · `storytree` alone lists the families.
1.6 · `storytree <family> <verb> --help` (or `-h`) prints that command's usage and summary and exits 0 without running it, even when the command needs arguments it was not given.

1.7 · A command or verb it does not have is refused (exit 2) naming the command for that job when agents are known to guess the word, else the nearest real one by spelling, and listing what the family has (ADR-0786 D3).
1.8 · An answer's `next:` offers only commands that open a record the answer just named or listed; no stock hints (ADR-0786 D2).

1.9 · `storytree --version` prints the 0.3.<n> of the build it comes from, the number the desktop app shows for that commit (ADR-0753 D2): from a source checkout, with its short commit; from an installed build, the release and commit stamped into it at packaging.

1.10 · Through `pnpm storytree` in a storytree checkout, a word arrives as written, holding double quotes, >, &, |, ^, %, backslashes or backticks, and nothing else runs or is written on its way (ADR-0851 D1).

reported.note: Commit 399163ab (.npmrc shell-emulator=true): the pnpm route prints exactly the door's own answer for the word, and no stray file is written. Windows, pnpm 9.15.0.

contracts.title: 1.11 · On Windows, a word the script shell still changes on its way (a $, a line break) is refused before the command runs: nothing is done, and the refusal names the word and says to pass that text from a file (ADR-0851 D2). On Linux and macOS pnpm 10 single-quotes each word, so such a word arrives as written.

reported.note: Commit 399163ab (packages/cli/src/handed.ts): refused before dispatch, naming word 1 and @<file>; by hand, a --answer holding $HOME was refused as word 5.

contracts.title: 1.12 · On Windows, a word given to the installed command whose double quotes the caller's own quoting changed, as Windows PowerShell 5.1 hands on a word holding a space and a double quote, is refused before the command acts, naming the word and saying to pass it from a file; a line quoted by Windows' standard rules (Git Bash, a program) is never refused (proven on Windows CI, skipped with a named reason elsewhere).

reported.note: Green on the laptop and on CI's Windows runner for storytree-ai/storytree#492: from Windows PowerShell 5.1 the word is refused before the command acts, naming word 1 and @<file>; from Git Bash the same word reaches the command. Skipped on Linux and macOS with its reason.

contracts.title: 1.13 · A comma-separated id flag containing whitespace inside an id is refused before any write, naming likely PowerShell array conversion and showing a quoted retry example without guessing or splitting ids; valid comma-separated lists preserve their ids.

1.14 · A flag value opening with @ is read from the file it names; one holding whitespace that names no file is prose kept as written (so text opening with a scoped package such as @storytree/cli reaches the record); a one-word @ value naming no file is refused, naming the path.

reported.note: packages/cli/src/at-values.test.ts '1.14 …' passes on main (ran in this lane's gate, PR #788 branch); health read untested only because no report was filed

contracts.title: 1.15 · A command kept waiting on the library (a connection slot on a full server, or another session's write) goes on when it can, says what it waits for on stderr as the wait starts when stderr is a person's terminal, and says nothing of it while stderr is captured

1.16 · In a folder whose marker names an existing project but is not approved as its checkout on this machine, a read and a write are refused before the project opens, naming `storytree doctor --join <project>`; after that join they work (ADR-0942 D1).
1.17 · every answer is recorded on the calling session as a door-answered line: the command, how it went, and the next steps offered as commands; an unknown word with the command its refusal named
1.18 · storytree doors prints the front-door reading for a window
1.19 · storytree lag prints Lag in real use's report over the lag readings kept in the storytree home
1.20 · `storytree settings show` lists the surfaces its story packages' manifests name, composed into its bundle by the plugin loader, and the same run unbundled: the forest's, then the arc surface's

1.21 · `storytree` mounts the families its story packages' manifests declare, in its bundle and run unbundled, each at the place it declares: the library's library 1st, CI health's health 18th, the arc surface's arc and question 2nd and 3rd, the library core's adr 4th with its guesses, Friction's friction and resteer 13th and 14th, the app setup's doctor 8th and setup, project and import 20th to 22nd, Processes' processes 24th, the Experiments story's experiment 27th, Session management's workspace among the rest, its bare name making a workspace, each listed in ascending order of its place, so a family at an unused or fractional place moves no other

1.23 · the command line mounts a declared family with the families within it, its aliases, its guesses and its retired words; a verb's many words and repeated flags, and every flag as a field, reach its work; a verb that writes is handed the writer the answer names once its work asks for it, a refusal names its next steps as commands, and a raw answer is printed as it is
1.24 · The command line mounts a callerless verb without opening the library, handing it the folder, script and journey runtime, and the shell's session when the shell names one alone

1.32 · A command the lane's experiment arm denies does nothing else: it exits 1 saying which experiment and arm deny it, and is recorded as a door-answered line with outcome denied-by-arm carrying the experiment and arm (ADR-1064 D2).
1.33 · A refused word offers, as next steps, the commands sessions ran after it was refused before
1.34 · the friction family's drain answers, then says what the doors learner did or why it did not run; every other family is mounted as it is
1.35 · a word pointed in its place runs the pointed command with the words after it, says it was pointed, and records an answered line carrying the word; a fallen pointer refuses again
1.36 · a word agents guess for a job a command already does runs that command with the words after it, and its answer says so

1.37 · A family whose story part is switched off on this computer (or stands on one that is) is not listed by `storytree`, and asking for it is refused saying it is switched off, because of which part, and the command that switches it on; the settings family stays mounted whatever is off
1.38 · `storytree doors learn --session <id>` runs the doors learner on the session it names, writing as that session, and refuses without one

1.39 · The command line opens the project with this computer's system switches: roles switched off are left out of `library list` and `library search` at the next command, `library read` still reads one by its id, a role switched on by its title shows again, and `settings show` lists what is off and on

1.40 · With a factory folder chosen and settings set part ci-health plugin my-health, the command line (bundled) lists and runs the factory plugin's family where ci-health's was, its verb handed the door's place; settings set part ci-health on mounts ci-health's own again

1.41 · With code review and architecture checks switched off, storytree starts and lists every family but theirs, asking for one says it is switched off, and project delete is handed no project records of theirs; with both on it is handed the QA ledger's
1.42 · The command line asks the arm checks its parts contribute; with none mounted, every command runs

1.43 · Everything the command line prints, answers and refusals alike, reaches the terminal with no control character but line breaks and tabs: a title holding an escape prints without its escape byte
1.44 · The command line opens the library with the kinds of record its mounted factory plugins declare
1.45 · A knowledge note a command writes from a session's shell carries what that session had read from outside in its history; from a shell whose session read none, no mark

1.46 · library list of a plugin kind this computer does not mount names the count, that it is dormant here, and the settings set part command that mounts it from this computer's factory, or that the factory has no such plugin

capabilities.title: 2 · Who wrote it
capabilities.description: Every write made through the command line is recorded as the person who ran it (their computer user name), so the library's history can tell a person's change from an agent's. When an agent runs the command from its own shell, the write is recorded as that agent's session instead (A1).

contracts.title: 2.1 · An edit through the command shows in the record's history as the person.
2.2 · The same edit, run with an agent session's id in the environment, shows as that session.
2.7 · A shell with STORYTREE_SESSION_ID acts as that session; with no session named, storytree processes refuses and says to set it

capabilities.title: 3 · Library
capabilities.description: Read any record whole, list a kind (optionally filtered by a field), search the artifacts, see what links to an artifact, and see a record's history of changes, all through the library's own reads. Write a new record of any kind, or edit named fields of one, with long text taken from a file, and a bad record is refused with the library's own message. Retire a record with a reason and its writer through the library's existing retire, preserving its refusals.

contracts.title: 3.1 · `read` returns the whole body.
3.2 · `edit` changes only the named fields.
3.3 · `new` without a required field is refused, naming it.

3.4 · `history` lists every write with its sequence, time, action, writer and reason; `--fields` also shows the stored fields after each write (the last state for retirement), so past values can be read after the fact.
3.5 · `list` shows only live records of the kind and filters by a field.
3.6 · `new memory` is refused with the reason that memories belong to the harness, and writes nothing (ADR-0650).
3.7 · `related <artifact> --unlinked` lists the artifacts most like it that no link reaches.
3.8 · `library retire <id> --reason <why>` retires any record the library permits, recording the reason and writer and returning the library's own refusals.
3.9 · `library search <words…> [--limit <n>]` shows the library's ranked answer (capability 14 of the library story), best first with scores, at most the limit; when it ranked by words it says why.
3.10 · `read <id> --field <name>` prints that one field exactly as stored and nothing else (a value that is not text, as JSON); a field the record does not have is refused, naming the fields it has.
3.11 · A list field given to `new` or `edit` as comma-separated ids is written as a list, from any shell; a shell-joined list is refused before writing, with the quoted retry.

reported.note: packages/cli/src/library.test.ts '3.11 …' (landed in PR #784) passes; ran in this lane's gate on PR #788's branch

contracts.title: 3.12 · library phrase returns a bounded JSON page of full records from the literal phrase API, accepts repeatable kind and field selections plus limit and after, preserves phrase whitespace, and gives a continuation cursor or a complete empty result.
3.13 · `library new check` writes a quality control check enforcing the principles or guardrails it names, and `library read` returns it whole.

3.14 · library edit and retire, run by a session holding an increment, hold a change to a story, capability or contract planned before it as a pending change on that increment, and library read of the increment lists each pending change as before and after, or its retirement
3.15 · `library new contract` numbers past the capability's contracts and the numbers its story package's numbered tests carry, as plan_contract does
3.16 · `new contract` with a title past 300 characters is written, and its answer adds an advisory quoting the library's definition of a contract; a shorter title gets none

3.17 · storytree import <folder> imports the folder into the project the command runs in, saying the mapped stories it added, retired and kept and, imported again, what moved since the last import; a refused folder is said with its reason

3.18 · `library read <id> <id>…` prints every record named, whole, in one start; `--linked` adds each record their id lists name (a role's rules and context, a note's links) once; an id with no record refuses the read, naming each, and prints none
3.19 · `library list` refuses a flag it does not read, before reading the library, naming --where <field>=<value> as the way to filter, and lists nothing
3.20 · library list friction leaves out resolved and dismissed reports unless --all, saying how many it left out; library search says each friction report's state
3.21 · `new contract`'s answer names the capability's other contracts that no numbered test carries yet, as plan_contract does

capabilities.title: 4 · Arcs and increments
capabilities.description: See the arcs, and one arc whole: its intent, end state, increments and their states, the questions waiting on you, and what each waiting item waits for. Create, edit, park or unpark an arc; park an increment, record a landing that was never parked, close one with its outcome, and make an arc or increment wait on another with a reason, or clear the wait.

contracts.title: 4.1 · An arc with no intent is refused.

4.2 · A close with no pull request needs a note. The correct-closure verb replaces a closed increment outcome with a required reason kept in history; it refuses open work, missing reasons and invalid outcomes without a write.
4.3 · A wait that would close a loop is refused, naming the loop, and nothing is written.
`arc show` names what each waiting increment waits for: the work it waits on, and each wait for you or an outside event with its note, check-back day, and "check-back passed" once that day has come.
4.5 · `arc list` names each live arc with the library's state, and the arcs closed yesterday or today; older closed arcs by a closing-day window (--closed today|yesterday|week, or --from and --to).
4.6 · Closing an increment ends its claim for any outcome, closed by its holder or the owner; a refused close, or one by another live session, leaves it held.

4.7 · `arc increment move <increment> --to <arc> --reason` re-homes an open or closed increment, keeping its id, lifecycle, outcome and any claim; without a reason, or for open work moving to a closed arc, it is refused.
4.8 · `arc show` reads the arc's view once and every hold in one ask, however many open increments the arc has: never a hold read per increment.

reported.note: arcView 1, holds 1, waitHolds 0, heldOnQuestion 0

contracts.title: 4.9 · `arc increment wait --for` makes an increment wait for you, or for an outside event until a check-back day, with a note, and `unwait --for` clears it; a wrong wait is refused readably, with nothing written

reported.note: arcs.test.ts 4.9, red then green, PR #818

contracts.title: 4.10 · `arc waits` lists every open increment's waits for you or an outside event across arcs, yours first by rank (1 first, the unranked after) with each one's why, then events by check-back day with the overdue flagged, from one read of the holds and one of the arcs; a wait for you on a parked arc is not listed but counted in one closing line naming its arcs (ADR-0835 D2)

reported.note: arcs.test.ts 4.10, red then green, PR #818

contracts.title: 4.11 · `arc show` says nothing of a wait whose blocker has landed: closing the blocker cleared it
4.12 · `arc increment unstart` returns an active increment nobody holds to proposal; a held, proposed or closed one is refused, naming why, with nothing written

4.13 · `arc increment edit --remedies` adds live friction to an increment's remedies, keeping those it had, so `friction route --to tool` accepts it; friction that is not live is refused with nothing written
4.14 · `arc increment wait --for owner` releases the waiting session's claims on the increment

4.15 · `arc increment new` and `edit` take --capabilities and --links, edit replacing each list; a story given as a capability is refused with nothing written, and the retired --touches is refused rather than ignored (ADR-0949 D2)

4.16 · `arc increment edit --capabilities` refuses a capability already on the list of another live session's claimed increment, naming that increment and its holder, with nothing written; the caller's own lists, and a released increment's, are not refused (ADR-0949 D2)
4.17 · `arc edit --priority` sets and clears an arc's priority, and `arc list` orders live arcs by it
4.19 · arc show says under each open increment how many pending plan changes it holds and the command that lists them, never the changes themselves

4.20 · `arc increment settle-pending` applies the leftover pending plan changes of every closed increment that landed and drops those of every one that did not, naming each increment and what it did, and says so when none is left

4.21 · `arc increment new --waits-on a,b --wait-reason <why>` parks an increment born waiting on each named increment; one flag without the other, or a blocker that is not an increment, is refused with nothing written
4.22 · `arc increment edit --held-on none` clears an increment's hold, and `--capabilities none` empties its capabilities list, as an empty value does where the shell delivers one
4.23 · `arc increment edit --machine <name>` names the one machine that can take an increment, `--machine none` clears it, and a name Machines does not know is refused with nothing written
4.24 · arc increment edit --capabilities lets the holder of a capability's claim list it, past a backed-off lane's list entry

4.25 · `arc increment new --wait-for owner --wait-note <text|@file> --wait-why <text|@file> [--wait-rank <n>]` parks an increment born waiting for the owner with that note, why and rank; one flag without the others it needs, a rank that is not a whole number from 1, or a releaser other than the owner, is refused with nothing written
4.26 · `arc increment drop-pending <increment> <record> --reason …` drops that one pending plan change from the open increment, saying which, and refuses a record the increment holds no change for

4.27 · `arc waits --audit` lists the owner actions that need attention, oldest read first, each with every reason: its note says "not yet" while nothing holds it, its note names an increment that has closed, it has no why, it has no rank, its arc is parked or closed, or it has not been read again in seven days

4.28 · `arc increment apply-pending <increment> --pr <n>` applies an open increment's pending plan changes under a merged pull request's mark, naming what it applied and what was stale, and refuses a pull request that has not merged, or a fork's, applying nothing

capabilities.title: 5 · Questions
capabilities.description: Raise a question for the owner on an arc (stakes, question, context, options, plus the analogy, diagram and recommendation 0.2 expected), optionally holding increments on it. Settle it with his answer in his words and the decision that carried it, retire one that was wrong, or list the open ones.

contracts.title: 5.2 · Settling needs an answer.
5.1 · A question with no stakes is refused.
5.3 · A held increment reads as waiting on you until its question is settled.

5.4 · `question retire` retires a question and releases every increment held on it in the same step, naming them; another record kind is refused without a write and points to `library retire`, which still refuses a question an increment is held on.
5.5 · `question list` lists open questions across arcs, or on one arc.
5.6 · `question check` says whether a question's review is fresh or lapsed; `question renew` re-stamps it, and renewing a settled question is refused.
5.7 · `library edit <question>` corrects an open question's wording in place; editing a settled question is refused, pointing at its standing answer.
5.8 · `question list` leaves out a parked arc's open questions, says how many wait there and on which arc, and that arc's own listing names them as parked with it
5.9 · `arc show` on a parked arc lists its open questions as parked with the arc, waiting for it to be unparked, not as waiting on you
5.10 · Unsupported question new flags are refused before any write, with the supported --hold option in the correction.

reported.note: Focused built CLI run passes all 11 question tests. 5.10 refuses --holds and --unknown before any recorded library change; 5.3 reads back the persisted --hold link.

contracts.title: 5.11 · `question show <id>` reads one question whole: its arc and state, what it asks, its options, analogy, diagram, recommendation and answer when given, and the open increments held on it; another record kind or a missing id is refused.
5.12 · `question new --hold` releases the asking session's claims on the held increment
5.13 · `question present` marks a question as being put to the owner by the calling session; another live session is refused, naming it, `question list` flags it, and `--done` frees it
5.14 · `question move` re-homes an open question on another arc, keeping its id and holders; a missing question or a refused move writes nothing

capabilities.title: 6 · Decisions
capabilities.description: List decisions (current, by status, load-bearing) and record a new one with an explicit `--number <n>` or the next number, its status, who decided it in their own words, and what it supersedes. In storytree, automatic numbers exceed the persisted floor and every number any record has ever held; omitting a number is refused if the floor is absent. Other projects start at 1. All numbering rules belong to the library; the CLI parses and reports them. Pull a decision out as a markdown file, edit it, push it back, and write its composed statement (the owner's C2). The one-time number, renumber (both modes), and set-floor commands have been retired after the completed N1 move.

contracts.title: 6.1 · In projects with automatic numbering, two `adr new` run at once get different, increasing numbers.
6.2 · Pull then push with no edit changes nothing.
6.3 · A superseded decision drops out of `--current`.
6.4 · A composed statement reads stale after its decision's text changes.
6.5 · `adr pull` names a decision by id, number, or ADR number.

6.6 · `adr new --number <n>` preserves an explicit unused number and refuses a reused or invalid number. In storytree, omitting the number is refused while the persisted decision number floor is absent; when present, omitting the number allocates above that floor and every number any record has ever held. Other projects continue to auto-number from 1.

capabilities.title: 10 · Plan view
capabilities.description:
`storytree tree` prints the plan as an indented tree: stories, capabilities and contracts, each with the health its agent reported (labelled as the agent's) and any claim on it. Name a story to see only that story.
`storytree capability built <capability>` says a capability is built, so it is no longer proposed, and `storytree capability proposed <capability>` says it is proposed again (ADR-0744 D2); both call the library's `setProposed`.

contracts.title: 10.1 · A story with capabilities and a contract prints in order with "agent says passing"; each capability title is printed as stored, with no list position added to its number.
10.2 · An unknown story says so.
10.3 · `capability built` switches a capability's proposed flag off and `capability proposed` back on, each with its writer; an unknown capability says so.
10.4 · `storytree tree` prints each capability's word, and for one that is not healthy its reason, who moves it and the contracts carrying it.

10.5 · `storytree health worklist` prints the oldest three capabilities on the health worklist, each with its word, reason, who moves it, the contracts carrying it and since when, and a failing one its verified note, and how many more wait; with none it says nothing waits. One a test run in progress will record is not offered: it is held back, counted, and the run named.

10.6 · In a project whose health nothing verifies, `storytree tree` gives each part the agent's report alone, and each built capability says storytree does not check this project's tests yet, never untested or a mover

10.7 · `storytree health worklist` says on a proposed capability's line when its tests already pass and only its proposed flag is left, and then offers `storytree capability built <capability>` as the next step

10.8 · `storytree tree`'s line for a mapped story says it is mapped, here before storytree and assumed to be working, with no health of its own (ADR-0993 D3); a capability planned on it keeps its own health line
10.9 · `storytree plan` prints what the show_plan tool answers: each story, capability and contract with its health, and the arcs; a window it cannot read is refused as the tool refuses it

10.10 · `storytree show`, the word agents reach for by the show_plan tool, prints the plan as `storytree plan` does; given a record's id it names `storytree library read <id>` and `storytree arc show <arc>`

10.11 · `storytree contract show <contract>` prints one contract with its reported and verified health, each with who wrote it, when and its note; `contract health` and `contract new` run the commands for those jobs; an id naming no contract says so

10.12 · `storytree contract report <contract> --result red|green [--note <text|@file>]` records what the report tool records: the contract's reported health, failing or passing, by the shell's harness and session, with the note, leaving the verified column untouched; a story, a capability, an unknown id or another result is refused and writes nothing; `contract --help` lists it

capabilities.title: 7 · Board, read only
capabilities.description: Show who is on what right now: each claim on an increment or a capability, with its agent's harness, window and reason, and whether it is live or idle; or who holds one piece of work. Claiming and releasing stay with the agents' tools.

contracts.title: 7.1 · A claim made through the agent tool appears with its harness and reason.
7.2 · An idle claim reads idle.
7.3 · `noticeboard <id>` names the holder, or "nobody".

7.4 · `noticeboard log [--session <id>] [--limit <n>] [--full]` shows the activity log's latest lines (20 unless told), each with its number, time, harness, session and what happened. Each names the line that caused it ("caused by #n"), or says "cause not recorded", never "no cause" (ADR-0746 D2). Default output clips long commands to 60 characters; --full preserves the complete recorded started and completed commands, including quotes and line breaks. Both forms keep the requested session and latest-line limit, and say when no matching lines exist.

capabilities.title: 8 · Doctor
capabilities.description: Run storytree's setup check from a terminal, the same one every agent session start runs: is storytree running, are the hooks registered and last seen firing, is this folder a project, is `storytree` on the path, is `gh` signed in, is Claude Code or Codex installed and signed in, and are git and a Node of at least 24 there. Run plain, it only looks: it changes no agent's hooks, status line or the `storytree` command, says what is missing or runs another build, and names the fix; `storytree doctor --repair` registers the hooks and status line and puts the command on the path. It sets a folder up as a project only when you tell it to.

contracts.title: 8.1 · With storytree closed, it opens it.
8.2 · With `gh` signed out, it notes what gh is for and that storytree works without it, and names no fix (ADR-0751).
8.3 · In a folder that is not a project, it creates nothing unless told to.
8.4 · A second run changes nothing.
8.5 · Setup installs the full command beside its hooks; the launcher reads the library and runs `doctor`; `setup remove` through the bundled command removes it again.

8.6 · With Codex's hooks registered and none run yet, the doctor names the one step that lets Codex run them, and from an administrator terminal that Codex cannot run commands there (agent link 8.16, 8.17).

reported.note: doctor.test.ts 8.5: red first (no Codex hooks line in the output), green once doctor prints the codex-hooks and elevated lines.

contracts.title: 8.7 · The doctor changes no agent's hook files unless told to repair; --repair registers them
8.8 · The doctor's exit code matches what it prints: 0 with its answer, 2 with the misuse it names

capabilities.title: 11 · Workspace
capabilities.description: `storytree workspace <increment> --reason <text>` makes a claimed Claude Code workspace, or prepares a Codex workspace by checking availability and fetching main. For Codex it prints the exact ref and name for the agent to pass to the app's `create_worktree`; the agent then runs `storytree workspace attach <increment> --folder <returned-directory> --ref <commit> --name <name> --reason <text>`. Storytree verifies the worktree and claims its branch; only the app creates the Codex folder. Both steps refuse held or waiting work, and only a running agent session may claim.

contracts.title: 11.1 · From a Claude Code agent's shell, `workspace <increment> --reason` makes a worktree on a fresh branch from `origin`'s main and claims the increment for that session on that branch, naming the folder to work in.
11.2 · Work another live session holds is refused naming its holder and the binding reason supplied by the agent link, and no worktree is made.
11.3 · From a shell no agent session runs, it is refused saying to run it from the agent, and nothing is claimed, for both preparation and attachment.

11.4 · From a Codex agent's shell, `workspace <increment> --reason` returns the exact freshly fetched commit and suggested name for the app's `create_worktree`, without creating a folder or claim. `workspace attach` with that ref, name and returned folder claims its verified branch for the same session and names the working directory. A bad directory is refused without a claim, explaining that the app's worktree is kept.
11.5 · `workspace release` ends the calling session's increment or capability claim without closing or landing the work.
11.6 · `workspace release` refuses another session's claim, an unheld target, and a shell without an agent session, without writing claim events.

11.7 · `session close-out --safe yes|no --why <text>` from an agent's shell records the calling session's close-out, which the sessions reading then carries, and lists every released claim id or explicitly says there were no claims to release; from a shell no agent session runs it is refused, and a --safe other than yes or no is refused as a usage error (ADR-0758 D2).
11.8 · Work with an open pull request is refused naming the --despite-open-pulls flag, and with that flag a workspace is made beside it

reported.note: workspace.test.ts passes all 11 tests. The new 11.8 regression uses openPulls despite changed wording and withholds retry advice without that data; the existing real CLI test proves refusal leaves no worktree/claim and --despite-open-pulls creates both.

contracts.title: 11.9 · `workspace claim <increment|capability> --reason` claims the work for the calling agent session without making a worktree or branch, and is refused as the claim tool refuses it, including the binding reason supplied for a held claim.

reported.note: workspace.test.ts 11.9: red (no verb 'claim') then green; PR #788

contracts.title: 11.10 · Work that waits for the owner or an outside event is refused naming what it waits for, its note and its check-back day

reported.note: workspace.test.ts 11.10, red then green, PR #818

contracts.title: 11.11 · `workspace release` of an increment's last claim returns the unclosed increment to proposal
11.12 · `workspace release --holder <session> --reason` is the session manager's release of a quiet session's claim; a live holder's claim is refused

11.13 · From a linked worktree, or a folder inside one, `workspace <increment> --reason` is refused with the agent link's hint to claim it there with `workspace claim`, making no worktree or branch and claiming or starting nothing, from Claude Code's and Codex's shells alike
11.15 · `workspace stale` lists each claimed increment whose holder is quiet, with its holder, last seen and route, and says when none is stale
11.16 · workspace allow is the user's yes, from their own terminal only
11.17 · workspace claim and attach take over a pull request's held claim on its own branch
11.18 · `workspace claim` takes several capabilities, as words or a comma list, all or nothing

capabilities.title: 12 · Check
capabilities.description: `storytree check`: a terminal front door onto the Guardrails story's check, so a user's CI and a person at a terminal run the package and allocation rules over their checkout.

contracts.title: 12.1 · `storytree check` exits 0 saying it passed on a checkout that keeps both rules, and 1 naming each problem on one that does not, in a folder that is no storytree project

capabilities.title: 14 · Reading the doors' use
capabilities.description: Counts a window of door-answered lines against the declared commands and tools: use per surface, misses, door share per step, follow per offered step with its like-for-like baseline, failures by class, each split by machine, harness and briefed or not.

contracts.title: 14.1 · Every declared command and tool is counted, those with none at zero
14.2 · Misses: each word refused as unknown, with the command named and the rate per 1,000 calls
14.3 · Follow per offered step, beside its like-for-like baseline
14.4 · Door share per step, and failures by class apart from refusals
14.5 · Split by machine, harness and briefed or not
14.6 · Reads a window from the project's activity log
14.7 · Each declared verb carries its consumers, and one a person may call is not judged by these lines
14.8 · Repoints: each word refused with hints, its offers, the hints followed by target, and none taken
14.9 · A refused word's repoint hints, learned from what sessions ran next after it
14.10 · a word refused at least 10 times in one place whose follows stay below the pointer bar is a want; a tool's name, stray text, a rarer word and one above the bar are not
14.11 · an agent-only verb with no call across 100 sessions in a covered window is a cut candidate by family; a twin unused in one door only is a gap, and a short or thin window cuts nothing
14.12 · the drain files a want as friction and raises a cut group as a question with an increment held on it, a second drain duplicates neither, and a project without the arcs learns nothing
14.13 · a want is filed on the learner's own branch, so it never spends the landing session's three, and one past the learner's three waits while the rest of the step runs
14.14 · a guessed word whose follows clear the bar is pointed to its leading target, once; a pointer its pointed calls mostly leave falls back, and only follows after a fallback count again
14.15 · the drain writes a word's pointer line once, with its evidence, and its fallback line once; a second drain writes neither again

14.16 · a drain a week or more after the last doors check reads the trailing week and files at most three standing-out items, skipping what the learner filed or raised, and records the check; a drain within the week does nothing

capabilities.title: 15 · The printed table
capabilities.description: Prints a reading for a person in a terminal (plain text, trailing 7 days with 28 beside it) and for a machine (--json), for the reconciliation increment.

contracts.title: 15.1 · Prints the reading as a plain-text table, the short window with the long beside it
15.2 · Prints the same readings as JSON
15.3 · Each command and tool is printed with its consumers, one with no call marked unused, or not judged when a person may call it
15.4 · Each refused word's hints are printed with its offers, the hints followed, and none taken

capabilities.title: 13 · Reading a command
capabilities.description: How the command line reads a declared verb's words and flags into its input and spells its usage (commandUsage, commandInput in packages/cli/src/command-input.ts), read the same as the MCP server reads a tool's arguments (toolInput, packages/mcp-server/src/tools/tool-input.ts), whose tests compare the two here since the command line is the one package that reaches both. Moved from Project and caller's 4 · The verb contract by ADR-1035 D2 (contracts 4.1, 4.2, 4.4, 4.5, 4.6 renumbered 13.x); the declaration schema itself is The library's 16 · The command schema. Earlier: Session management's sessions/verb.ts, moved by ADR-1025 D5 with contract 4.31.

contracts.title: 13.1 · A verb declared once reads a command's words and flags and a tool's arguments to the same input, refuses the same wrong input on both, and does the same work and answers in the same sentence for either door

13.2 · A text input marked optional may be left out on either door and reads as nothing; a verb's command may give the usage its inputs cannot spell, and a family may declare the verb its bare name runs

13.4 · A text input may be many, each word from its place on or each repetition of its flag, and none when optional; an open set of fields takes every flag the other inputs do not name; a verb may declare that it writes and answer raw
13.5 · A command's stray words and flags are refused as misuse, the flag named and a word never echoed
13.6 · A text input marked blank keeps a value that says nothing, read as empty, on either door; a refusal may name the steps that do the job instead
13.7 · A text input marked verbatim keeps its value as given, its leading and trailing whitespace included, on either door
13.8 · A count input is a whole number above 0, left out only when optional, and a fields input marked json takes any JSON value, a command's read as JSON where it parses, on either door

stories.title: Knowledge graph
stories.description: The project's notes and decisions drawn inside the globe, below the stories and capabilities that reference them, with replaced decisions as ghosts and the notes a session read lit up. Owns packages/knowledge-core.

depth.reason: no depth flag in its code

radius.reason: 6 packages downstream; public users, inherited from packages/website

capabilities.title: 2 · Earlier decisions beside their replacements
capabilities.description: A replaced decision appears as a see-through ghost beside the decision that replaced it, and lights when its recorded reader reaches it. Its card tells an explicit supersession from an earlier cover found in write history. Proposed decisions stay out of this first slice.

contracts.title: 2.1 · An accepted decision that explicitly supersedes an old one makes a ghost, even when the old front-cover mark was never cleared. A proposal naming an old decision does not supersede it.

2.2 · For older records, a new cover on the same shelf linking to the old one, followed by clearing the old cover's mark, makes an "earlier cover" ghost when the replacement is unique. Clearing a mark alone, editing the wording, or merely linking to an old decision does not.
2.3 · A unique chain of replacements ends beside its current successor. A missing or ambiguous successor gets an outer ghost labelled "replacement not placed", rather than a guessed home.

2.4 · Depth and incoming-link sizes use only artifacts that are neither ghosts nor proposed; replacement relations are not support links. A ghost never changes that layout, and its own visit count stays inspectable.
2.6 · The Library leaves out friction reports whose state is resolved or dismissed; open and routed ones, and ones with no state stored, stay

capabilities.title: 1 · Knowledge under its shelves
capabilities.description: The project's artifacts hang below the stories' and capabilities' front covers, with depth counting the longest chain of references from any shelf. A shared artifact appears once, a loop is drawn as a labelled error, and an artifact no shelf reaches has "no depth". On the globe, shelf-placed knowledge is drawn beneath its islands. Story-text definitions are excluded from the drawing; the remaining no-shelf artifacts fill a ball within 0.55 globe radii, separated from one another and shelf points by at least 0.035 radii (ADR-0661 D3). Forest shows the core beneath the story nodes; Library shows it alone on the same globe (ADR-0660 D4). The separate Look-inside view stays unmounted.

contracts.title: 1.1 · With a cover A, links A → B → C and a shortcut A → C, C stays at depth 3: the shelf-to-cover step counts as 1. Visits and incoming-link counts never change that depth.

1.2 · An artifact reached by two shelves appears once, at its greatest depth, and names both entrances. A front cover keeps its own shelf as its home, and another shared artifact hangs under the oldest reachable shelf, with a stable tie-break.

1.3 · With A → B → C → B and C → D, B and C share a loop marked as an error at group depth 2, and D is at 3. An unreachable loop, like any unreachable artifact, is classified as no shelf, with no depth.
1.4 · Forty covers on their shelves and five artifacts on none, with no links, give forty artifacts at depth 1 and five with no shelf route, with no invented links. An empty shelf says it is empty.

capabilities.title: 8 · Setup check
capabilities.description:
The only thing the user installs is the storytree tool server, once, with the one-line command Claude Code or Codex already uses for any MCP server, and after that every session start checks storytree's setup and fixes whatever is missing on the spot. It opens storytree if it is closed, registers the hooks if they are missing (walking Codex users through Codex's one-time approval), and in a folder that isn't a storytree project yet it asks the user, through the agent, whether to set one up. It also says whether Claude Code or Codex is signed in and whether git and a usable Node are there, naming the fix for each that is missing, and never waits on a tool that does not answer (ADR-0716). It registers hooks for each harness home it finds except a harness the user disconnected from storytree (the app setup's contract 2.5), which gets its hooks back only when it is connected again. It also puts the `storytree` command on the user's path (contract 8.9): a shell script, or on Windows a small program of its own that hands each word on as the caller's command line spelled it (ADR-0854).

As built (increment_e0065ed16d5a, PR #452, contract 8.20): check_setup asks the agent to write its check file with its own file-editing tool: since 8.39 (increment_ff1771935a13) that is storytree-check-<session> in the system's temporary folder, named in the answer's text and its data's checkFile, so the user's repository never holds it; the harness may ask the user to allow a write outside the project. Once this session's edit hook has arrived, each check file it names is deleted at the recorded path, resolving relative paths against that hook line's folder, including a worktree different from the tool server's folder, even while other hooks are missing. A file the operating system refuses to remove stays for the agent. A leftover stays in the temporary folder, where it troubles no one.

contracts.title: 8.1 · In a throwaway home with only the tool server installed, the first session start registers the hooks for Claude Code and for Codex without touching any other setting.
8.2 · A second start changes nothing, and removing storytree takes out exactly what it added.
8.3 · With storytree closed, a session start opens it.

8.4 · In a folder that is not a project, check_setup says the folder is not a storytree project and that the user can add it (Add project in the app, `storytree doctor --set-up <name>`, or asking their agent), without telling the agent to offer setup (ADR-0752 D3), and nothing is created until the user asks. A successful yes creates the project and folder marker, then durably records that project as the user's choice for the app. A refused or failed setup does not report success or change the remembered choice; if saving the choice fails, the folder marker is restored to its previous state so the explicit setup can be retried. An ordinary session start, an existing-project setup check, or a repeated setup tool call in an already configured folder records no choice. The setup tools' input and output shapes remain the same (ADR-0657 D3).

8.5 · The agent fires a test of each hook (a session start, a call to a storytree tool, a file edit, a command), and the connection shows as verified only when storytree has received every one. Until then it names the missing hook and the fix, such as Codex's one-time approval.

8.6 · Live check: a real Claude Code session and a real Codex session, each in a new empty folder set up as a project by the installer's folder step (or `storytree doctor --set-up`), with nothing else configured by hand, and told "add a sign-up form, with tests", show up live, plan, claim, report red then green and land, and the agent activity log and the library show all of it. A second session that ignores storytree and only edits a file shows up as unplanned activity. *Subscription-billed: run once, as the final proof.*

capabilities.title: 1 · Get storytree
capabilities.description:
One command gets the Windows app and the tools its agent needs onto the computer, ready to run without a storytree checkout. Running it again reuses a working installation or explains what failed and how to retry.

As built: the release publishes install-storytree.ps1, its PowerShell one-liner and a version-matched SHA-256 manifest alongside the existing combined Windows x64/arm64 NSIS installer. Desktop packaging ships a native pinned Node 24 runtime, the complete agent-link buildBins output including imported chunks, a delivery helper and Node's license in resources/agent-tools. Delivery verifies and reuses a working installation before contacting the feed, explicitly launches its executable to show a hidden window or establish the first app launch, and waits for the app-owned database. It records stable installed tool paths in the 0.3 home's delivery.json and puts its CLI wrapper on the per-user Windows PATH; unrelated storytree commands are preserved and named. Failed steps include a retry action, incomplete existing apps are retained with repair/update instructions, and delivery does not create projects, change harness settings, install a developer toolchain, or touch 0.2. Ordinary updates remain the app's existing NSIS update route and replace the tool payload at the same paths. setup install retains its existing hook/command meaning; capability 2 owns connection.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/deliver/README.md. Linux tests use temporary homes, fake app launch/readiness and real PowerShell orchestration with injected effects; the actual built CLI, hook, setup, delivery helper and MCP server run outside a checkout. Both Windows runtime downloads match pinned SHA-256 values and their PE architectures. Windows CI additionally checks the installed x64 tool payload from a path with spaces. These proofs do not attest real first-ever/hidden-window startup, fresh-terminal registry propagation, interrupted NSIS installation, native arm64 execution, a live release update with active agent processes, or the agent-link 8.6 two-harness walkthrough; those remain the laptop acceptance lane.

As built (ADR-1162, contract 1.15): once delivery is ready the one-liner asks nothing. Its first line after the install says the app is open and gives the terminal command that opens it again; connecting agents and adding a project are the app's first-run guide (capability 3). `storytree setup connect` still connects from a terminal through delivery.json and capability 2's registration functions. Tools registration is never presented as hooks verified. Evidence of the earlier prompt: packages/app-setup/evidence/join/README.md.

As built (ADR-0854): on Windows the installed command is `storytree.exe`, a 5 KB program of its own built with LLVM from the agent link's launcher source and shipped in the payload as `storytree-launcher.exe`, so no shell reads its words: from Git Bash, Windows PowerShell or a program that starts it, each word reaches the CLI as the caller's command line spelled it (contract 1.9). The batch file it was before, `storytree.cmd`, is replaced by it in its folder. Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/native-launcher/README.md.

As built (groundwork for the macOS arc, arc_5b467265f126, contract 1.11): the delivery API also stages Apple Silicon's runtime. `macRuntime("arm64")` pins Node 24.21.0's darwin-arm64 archive and its bin/node hash, and `stageRuntime` extracts that executable with mode 755, refusing any checksum mismatch and keeping the previous runtime. `writePayloadManifest` takes the platform: a Mac payload needs `node` and no Windows launcher. `toolPaths`/`verifyPayload` read a .app bundle's Contents/Resources/agent-tools and Contents/MacOS/storytree-0.3. macOS packaging, the shell install and notarisation are the arc's later increments. Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/deliver/README.md.

As built (Linux arc, arc_38613dac8d7c, contract 1.13): the same curl | sh one-liner installs on x64 Linux. install.sh refuses another chip, names the one apt command for a missing libfuse2 (it never runs sudo), takes the release's AppImage by its checksum from storytree-delivery.json's linux.x64 entry, and installs a folder ~/.local/share/storytree-0.3 holding the AppImage as storytree-0.3, its resources/agent-tools extracted beside it (so toolPaths(dir, "linux") reads it unchanged and the hooks' Node path stays put) and its icon, plus a menu entry in ~/.local/share/applications whose Exec starts the installed AppImage with the arguments the release packaged. The installed version is read from the AppImage's own desktop entry (X-AppImage-Version), extracted without FUSE. The PATH line goes in ~/.profile; the command itself is the helper's ~/.storytree/0.3/bin/storytree, as on a Mac. The helper runs from x64 Linux's payload. The Linux release runner writes storytree-delivery-linux.json, merged into the manifest on publish. Not proved here: a launch and database start in a real desktop session, and the Ubuntu 24.04 sandbox question; those are the Mint acceptance increment's.

contracts.title: 1.1 · On a clean Windows x64 machine and an arm64 machine, the PowerShell one-line command delivers the matching app, a bundled Node runtime and a runnable tool-server, hook, setup and command-line bundle, including its imported chunks.

1.2 · The first-run journey displays the app and reaches its database both without a previous launch record and when the app is already running with its window hidden, without a separate manual "open once" step.
1.3 · Repeating the command in the same or a second folder reuses the installation without replacing user settings or touching 0.2's installation or data, and creates no project.
1.4 · An interrupted or refused installation reports the failed step and a retry action, without announcing a working connection or replacing the last usable installation.

1.5 · After the app takes an ordinary release update, the next agent session still starts compatible tools from a durable location, without rebuilding a checkout or relying on a package-manager cache.
1.6 · The installed command runs from a fresh Windows terminal; an existing unrelated `storytree` command is preserved and the conflict is named.

1.8 · Uninstalling from Windows Apps & features (or `storytree setup uninstall`) removes everything storytree added. That is the app, its command and PATH entry, this installation's agent registrations, hooks and status line in Claude Code and Codex, the update cache and its home. It asks first whether to keep the local library (kept, only the library stays). The user's project folders, other agent settings and another installation's home stay untouched, and an app update removes nothing.

1.9 · On Windows, the installed command hands each word on as the caller's command line spelled it, through no shell: run by name from Git Bash, Windows PowerShell or a program that starts it, a word holding >, &, |, % or ^ arrives unchanged, as does an inner double quote from Git Bash or a program; nothing else runs and no file is written (ADR-0854; proven on Windows CI, skipped with a named reason elsewhere).

capabilities.title: 2 · Connect an agent
capabilities.description:
The user chooses Claude Code, Codex or both, and storytree connects its installed tools to those agents. The next session uses the existing setup check to ask about the project and show whether the connection actually works.

As built: @storytree/app-setup/connect exports connectAgents and disconnectAgents for the chosen harnesses, with installedToolServerCommand(bundledNodePath, installedMcpScriptPath) as the delivery seam. Registration is per user, keeps unrelated settings and old entries, uses the existing storytree MCP name, and reports incompatible entries without overwriting. It captures no project or working directory. Repeating it leaves the compatible entry untouched. Missing harnesses, invalid settings, missing installed tools and failed writes produce separate recovery results for each harness.

As built: disconnect removes the selected registration and only hooks matching this installation, preserving other commands in mixed groups and any other installation's hooks. It keeps the shared command until no connection remains and removes only the matching launcher. A disconnected harness stays disconnected: disconnect records it in the storytree home (disconnected-harnesses.json), and the setup check, run from the other harness's sessions, registers no hooks for it until Connect connects it again. Installation results distinguish tools registration from hooks not verified; the existing setup check owns project consent and received-event verification. Connect also registers the chosen harness's hooks (and Claude Code's status line), never the unchosen one's, so the first session after installing already runs the start hook that asks the setup question; before this, hooks arrived only when that first session's tool server ran the setup check, too late for its own start. Registering is still not verifying: results keep saying "hooks not verified" until the setup check has received each event.

contracts.title: 2.1 · Choosing either harness or both registers the installed tool server per user for the chosen harnesses, preserving other servers, settings and any existing 0.2 entry.
2.2 · A new agent session in the invoking folder, and later in another folder, reaches that folder's existing setup check rather than a fixed installer directory or a hard-coded project.
2.3 · Repeating registration leaves one effective storytree entry per chosen harness; an incompatible existing entry is explained instead of silently overwritten.
2.4 · A missing harness or an invalid settings file gets a specific recovery action and no success claim for that harness; a successful registration for the other harness is reported separately.

2.5 · Disconnecting one harness keeps the other's connection and the shared command working; removing all connections cleans up only storytree-owned registrations, hooks and command, keeping project libraries and unrelated settings.

2.6 · The installation result tells "tools connected" apart from "hooks verified"; a missing hook stays named by the existing setup check until its event is received. For Codex it says whether its hooks run or wait for the user to trust them, naming the one step while they wait, and, from an administrator terminal, that Codex cannot run commands from one.

2.9 · Codex, which hides a tool server's instructions and tools until the agent searches for them, is told through the AGENTS.md in its home to call check_setup before its first change in a storytree project, and to ignore storytree in any other folder: one marked section, written again changes nothing, the user's own text kept, removed exactly.

capabilities.title: 3 · First-run guide
capabilities.description:
A short in-app guide tells the user what to do next, what storytree will ask, and what a working first project looks like. They can reopen it when adding another project or recovering from a connection problem.

As built: @storytree/app-setup/view mounts one Help entry outside the project surface, available with no project, either forest or a library error. First launch offers the guide; dismissal is remembered locally and Help reopens it. The guide covers the chosen agent, explicit project consent, harness approval, received-hook verification, first visible work, a second project, the unsigned Windows installer and feedback. Since ADR-1162 the guide's first section sets up the computer, both steps optional: it lists each coding agent the computer runs (capability 2's agentsOnThisComputer), connected or with its own Connect, which connects through delivery.json's tools or the app's own, and offers Add a project… through the same folder picker as New project… (contract 3.13). Check a folder calls the agent link’s public runSetupCheck and displays its diagnostic lines and fixes. The adjacent copy action prepares a check_setup request for the agent; this folder check does not install hooks or the command and cannot verify hook receipt. The app’s existing projectSelection/followProjects refresh remains responsible for the project list.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/help/README.md. Headless Chromium exercises the actual renderer and isolated library, including two setup fixtures and both selectable forests. Contract 3.3’s real two-empty-folder/two-yes harness walkthrough and the final installer handoff remain Windows acceptance work.

contracts.title: 3.1 · Completing installation offers the in-app guide without requiring a project to exist, and its entry point opens it again later.
3.2 · From the guide, the user can reach the existing setup diagnostics and their recovery action when the connection is incomplete.

3.3 · The guide says how to add a project three ways (the app's Add project, `storytree doctor --set-up <name>` in a terminal, or asking the agent in the folder); a project added any of these ways appears in the running app and both forests are selectable.

3.4 · Add project in the app's Projects section or the first-run guide, or started from the app bar's "New project…", opens the native folder picker; the chosen folder becomes a project under its own name (a name already taken by another project gets `-2`, `-3`…, so a second folder never joins an existing project silently), set up as the setup check's yes sets one up (marker, library project, the app's project choice), and is shown. A folder already in a project is simply selected; cancelling the picker changes nothing (ADR-0752 D2). One picker at a time.

3.5 · The first-run guide shows, each time it opens, that Codex waits for the user to trust storytree's hooks, with the one step, until one has run, then that it runs them; with no Codex hooks it says nothing of Codex.

contracts.title: 3.7 · Remove, in the app's Projects section or with `storytree project remove <name>`, takes a project added by mistake off this computer's list and frees its folder here (a marker git tracks is left and named); its records stay in the library, and a deliberate join, or adding its folder here again, brings it back as the same project, never a `-2`. An unknown name is refused.

3.6 · Delete, in the app's Projects section or with `storytree project delete <name> --confirm <name>`, drops a project's records for every computer using the library once its name is typed, after saying where they live and who loses them; a snapshot into this computer's backups is taken first unless skipped, and restores it. On POSIX, that snapshot is private from its first write (0700 backup directories, including existing ones, and a new 0600 file), independent of the home permissions or umask. On Windows, owner-only ACLs protect both backup directories (including existing ones) and the exclusively created snapshot before any snapshot bytes, even under permissive inherited permissions; an unrelated non-administrative user cannot read it, and the same user can restore it. Failure to establish privacy or save it leaves the project intact. Its activity lines, transcripts and QA ledger rows go with it, and a computer that had hidden it forgets the name, so a later project of that name starts clean and is shown. Refused for a wrong name, the project in use (on show in the app here, or the one the command's folder belongs to), and while a live session holds a claim in it.
