contracts.title: 5.1 · `storytree health local`, on the command line only (it has no MCP tool), runs the project's own tests by its package.json test command in the project's folder, which needs no git repository, and records each numbered test's verdict on its story's promise as a local test run: passing when its tests pass, failing once one fails; a project with no test command writes nothing and says why, and so does one whose CI storytree reads (a GitHub origin with a workflow), which points to health ci instead

stories.title: Architecture checks
stories.description: A project, or storytree itself, is held to its structural rules (each package belongs to one story, dependencies run one way, every source file is reached by a numbered test), reported by `storytree check` from the checkout alone. Owns packages/guardrails.

depth.reason: no depth flag in its code

radius.reason: 8 packages downstream; public users, inherited from packages/website

capabilities.title: 1 · The package rule
capabilities.description: Refuses a checkout that breaks the package rule: a story with no package or declared with several (each story owns exactly one, ADR-1071 rule 5), a package that is no story's, a story's code in a declared frame or front door, a reach into another story's files, workspace packages depending on each other in a cycle, and a story depending on a declared frame or front door unless the owner sanctioned that edge; a sanctioned edge no package.json uses is reported.

contracts.title: 1.1 · A story with no package is refused, and so is a package that belongs to no story (in a project that declares no stories, every package under packages/ is a story's).

1.2 · A story's code in a declared frame or front door is refused; a frame test reaching the story through its package passes; a refused file that leans on the frame is never told to move into the story's package.
1.3 · A package reaching into another story's files is refused, by relative path or by a subpath its package.json does not export.

1.4 · Workspace packages depending on each other in a cycle, even through a devDependency, are refused (roads run one way). Each distinct cycle is reported once; shared acyclic paths are checked without path enumeration, including paths leading into a cycle.
1.5 · A story depending on a declared frame or front door is refused, naming the edge, unless the owner sanctioned it in the edge list; a sanctioned edge no package.json uses any more is reported.
1.6 · A story owns exactly one package: a story declared with several is refused, and the package it would add belongs to no story

capabilities.title: 2 · The allocation rule
capabilities.description: Fails a checkout that leaves a story package's source file reached by no numbered test, naming each such file with its lines and the three ways out (number a test, plan a contract, delete the code).

contracts.title: 2.1 · A story package's source file that no numbered test reaches (by import, or by its coverage map survey-coverage.json) fails, named with its lines and the three ways out; reached, it passes; a test with no number allocates nothing.
2.2 · A source file whose opening comment declares a capability its numbered tests and coverage map do not reach fails, naming the file, its declaration and the capabilities that do reach it
2.3 · Asked to, a source file whose opening comment declares no capability fails, naming the file and suggesting the capability the survey infers for it
2.4 · A refused file whose package's coverage map has no entry for it is also told to re-measure that map with pnpm survey:coverage <package>; a package with no map, or a map holding the file, is not

2.5 · Guardrails contributes its allocation rule as a claim check: for a capability, the source files of its story's package no numbered test reaches; none for a capability the plan lacks (ADR-1170 D2)

capabilities.title: 3 · The check command
capabilities.description: `storytree check`, run in a checkout, runs the package rule and the allocation rule over it and reports every failure plainly, exiting non-zero, or says it passes and exits zero. It reads the checkout alone.

contracts.title: 3.1 · `storytree check` run in a checkout reports every package-rule and allocation failure plainly and exits non-zero; a checkout that keeps both rules prints that it passes and exits zero.
3.2 · It needs no plan, library or running app: it reads the checkout alone.
3.3 · Run from storytree's source on a folder, as a user's CI runs it, the check prints its report and exits 1 when either rule is broken, 0 when both are kept

3.9 · The storytree check job Guardrails contributes to a user's pipeline installs only what the check runs on, runs no install script, so a download it never uses cannot fail it, and asks for the checkout's history
3.4 · A project whose package depends on an imported app outside it, by link: and deep file paths, passes the check; a rule broken inside the project still fails it
3.5 · `storytree check` reads the frames a checkout declares in its storytree.check.json: a package in a declared frame passes the package rule, one in no story and no declared frame fails it
3.6 · `storytree check` reads the sanctioned edges a checkout declares in its storytree.check.json: a sanctioned story-to-frame edge passes the package rule, an unsanctioned one fails it
3.7 · Guardrails declares the `check` verb the command line mounts: run with no caller, in a folder that is no project, it answers with the check's report and refuses with it when a rule is broken

3.8 · `storytree check` runs the graduated self-equal assertion check on what the branch changes against origin/main: a test asserting an expression equal to itself fails the check, named by file and line; without origin/main it says the check did not run, never that it was kept
3.10 · The storytree check job fetches storytree's source at exactly the commit it is given and stops before running when what it checked out is any other

capabilities.title: 4 · Graduated checks
capabilities.description: Deterministic checks on a change, run from a checkout far more often than CI runs. Each is all of a quality control check, or the part of one that is a fixed pattern, graduated from the Quality assurance story's reviewer (ADR-0956 D5). Run on the files a branch changes against origin/main, it reports every place a graduated check trips, by the check's name, the file and the line. It reads the checkout alone and records nothing: Guardrails does not reach the library, so Quality assurance runs it and records its hits in the QA ledger. If this capability grows too big it becomes its own story (ADR-0956 D5).

contracts.title: 4.1 · Run on a change in a checkout (the files its branch changes against origin/main), each graduated check reports every place it trips, with the check's name, the file and the line (for example a constant asserted equal to itself); a change that trips none reports none, and a tripping line in a file the change does not touch is not reported.
4.2 · It needs no plan, library or running app and writes nothing: it reads the checkout alone, and what it found is its answer, for the caller to record.

capabilities.title: 5 · The placement report
capabilities.description: Rule 5 of the story rules (the journey principle, ADR-1078), counted at the package level as ADR-1085 D3 narrows it. For each package of a checkout it counts the other packages whose production code imports it, type-only imports included, as the map's code survey reads them. Delivery mechanisms (the front-door frames, and the composition root the checkout declares) and plumbing calls (forwarders the survey detects; build steps and cleanups the checkout declares) are listed but not counted. It says the placement each count implies, and names each package placed differently from today, with the loop a move would make. `storytree check` prints it, and it never fails the check. Its settings live in the checkout's storytree.check.json: the threshold, the composition root, the declared plumbing, and off.

contracts.title: 5.1 · A package's counted callers are the other packages whose production code imports it, type-only imports included; tests and testing helpers make none
5.2 · The front-door frames' imports and the declared composition root's are listed as delivery mechanisms, not counted
5.3 · A forwarder the code survey detects, and a build step or cleanup storytree.check.json declares, is listed as plumbing by its kind, not counted

5.4 · Each count implies a placement: at or above the threshold its own story, one caller inside that story, none its own story, between them separate ways; a package placed differently from today is named, with the loop moving it would make
5.5 · storytree check prints the placement report and never fails on it; placement off leaves it out

stories.title: Code review
stories.description: A change is reviewed before the gate by a fresh-context reviewer against the quality checks and its contracts, and every finding is recorded in the QA ledger and answered. Owns packages/quality-assurance.

depth.reason: flags: additive schema, fix loop, record writes

radius.reason: 6 packages downstream; public users, inherited from packages/website

capabilities.title: 1 · Quality control checks
capabilities.description: A quality control check is one question a reviewer can answer yes or no about a finished change (for example: is any expected value computed the way the code computes it?). Each is its own artifact in the library, of the kind the library declares for it (the library story, Knowledge artifacts), linked to the principle or guardrail note it enforces; the notes stay, carrying the reason for the rule (ADR-0956 D3). This capability gives the checks as one reading, for the change-reviewer and for people, the same from both front doors.

contracts.title: 1.1 · The checks reading gives every live check with its question and, for each note it enforces, that note's id, kind and title; a retired check is not in it.

1.2 · The command line and the agent link's tool give the same checks reading, each through this package's public API; the tool is the one this package registers on the agent link's server, which serves it, and the review loop's tools, for every project, storytree's own or a user's.

1.3 · Quality assurance declares the `quality` verbs the command line mounts: `quality checks` answers with the checks reading, and a verb that needs the ledger is refused when the door hands no server

capabilities.title: 2 · Change review
capabilities.description: The review of one change (one increment's branch) by the `change-reviewer` role, run as an ordinary subagent with a fresh context once the change is green and before the gate (ADR-0956 D1). This capability makes what the reviewer reads, the review brief: the branch's diff against origin/main, the contracts of the capabilities the increment names, and the live checks, with nothing of the implementer's reasoning. And it takes what the reviewer returns: for every check, whether the change trips it and where; for every contract, whether the change does what it says. The role's own text is an agent role in the library, a note, and is not contracted here.

contracts.title: 2.1 · The brief for a change's first review holds the branch's diff against the default branch origin names (origin/main when it names none), every contract of the capabilities its increment names, and every live check with its question, and nothing else: the increment's own body is not in it.

2.2 · A review's return is taken only when it answers every check in its brief (tripped or not, and where tripped: the file, the line and what was found) and every contract in it (met or not, and why not); a return that leaves one unanswered, or answers one the brief did not hold, is refused, naming it, and nothing is recorded.

2.3 · The command line and the agent link's tools issue the same brief and take the same return, each through this package's public API; the brief's tool takes the change's diff, or the worktree to read it from, as an argument, since the agent link's folder is not the branch.

2.4 · A contract the increment rewords through a pending change is in its brief in the pending text, marked pending, and one it retires through a pending change is listed as retired with its reason and is not to be answered; a return that answers a retired one is refused, naming it. Each appears in the brief once: its plan change is not listed again among the pending plan changes, so a return answering it once is taken.
2.5 · The brief lists each contract under its story and capability, so two stories' contracts sharing a number both appear, each with its story
2.6 · The diff read from a worktree holds its uncommitted work too, edits and new files Git does not ignore; a folder whose origin names no default branch is read against its own commit

2.7 · In a repository with no origin/main the brief's diff is read against its local default branch (init.defaultBranch, else main, else master), and the brief names that branch as the repository's own
2.8 · The brief reads the change from the worktree on the branch its increment was claimed on, wherever the brief runs, and is refused naming that branch when no worktree is on it
2.9 · A return names the review it answers, and take refuses one naming another review, such as a return left from an earlier review, recording nothing
2.10 · A plan-only change, whose diff touches no file, gets a brief listing its pending plan changes as the thing under review; one with neither a diff nor a pending change is still refused
2.11 · A low-tier change gets a light pass, judged from its diff alone; medium, high or an unread tier gets the full brief

2.12 · The brief lists each change-triggered guardrail of the stories and capabilities the increment names; the return answers each passed or failed with pictures, and a failed one stands until a later review passes it

2.13 · A return says of each contract whether the change touches it; a touched contract answered met names the test that covers it, or is taken as a hit at the changed line asking for one, and one the change adds or rewords cannot be answered untouched
2.14 · A new test with no saved red run naming it failing is a hit
2.15 · A red run saved in another worktree counts when its commit is in this worktree's history
2.16 · `quality brief` and `take` review a change in a named checkout outside the project, as the owner's factory repo is, and record it in the project's ledger

2.17 · A check that names the projects it applies to is in the brief only of a change in one of those projects; a check that names none is in every project's brief, so a user's project, reading its factory's checks, is not asked storytree's own

2.18 · The brief of a change to a factory plugin's story carries the factory branch's diff and the plugin plan's contracts, refuses to count them met when that branch is unread, and reads the plugin crossed only when no branch carries the change
2.19 · `quality brief --also <folder>`, given once per checkout, lists each outside checkout's diff beside the change's own in one brief, and `quality take --also` runs the graduated checks there too
2.20 · A test a factory worktree's or an --also checkout's diff adds is listed with whether that checkout's saved red runs name it failing, and one none names is a hit

reported.note: passing with the change

contracts.title: 2.21 · A test that only moved or was renumbered is not a new test
2.22 · The brief lists the library records the increment's sessions wrote since claiming it, as part of the change under review

2.23 · A check's answer may name places without tripping it, each with its file, line and what it is; the take keeps them in the return and prints them under their check, and refuses a named place with no file, line or words

capabilities.title: 3 · QA ledger
capabilities.description:
The record of what quality control finds, kept in the library's Postgres (ADR-0956 D4). Every review records, for each check it ran, whether it hit, and for each hit the implementer's answer: fixed, or rejected with a reason. Rows are scoped by check, project and package from the first row, because products differ in shape and a global count hides where a check matters. Its reading gives the counts per check per package, the same from both front doors. It only records: nothing here samples, reduces or retires a check (ADR-0956 D6).

Not settled by this plan (2026-10-10, raised with the dispatching session): where the rows sit inside the library's Postgres, as a record type the library declares, or as this story's own tables reached through the library's connection, as the agent link's activity log is. The contracts hold either way.

contracts.title: 3.1 · Recording a review writes, for each check it ran and each package the change touches, that the check ran there and each hit it made (the file and the line), with the review, the project and the time; a check that ran and did not hit is recorded as ran, and a second connection to the library's Postgres reads the rows back.

3.2 · The implementer's answer is recorded on a hit as fixed, or as rejected with its reason; a rejection with no reason, and an answer to a hit the ledger does not hold, are refused and nothing is written; a hit not yet answered reads unanswered.

3.3 · The ledger's reading gives, for each check and each package of a project, how many reviews ran it, how many hits it made, and those hits by answer (fixed, rejected, unanswered); a check that ran and never hit reads ran with no hits, never absent, and another project's rows are never counted.
3.4 · The command line and the agent link's tool give the same ledger reading, each through this package's public API; the tool is the one this package registers on the agent link's server.
3.5 · The project records this package contributes through its manifest's projectRecords forget a project's ledger runs and hits as it is deleted, and leave another project's

capabilities.title: 4 · Review loop bound
capabilities.description: A review may loop: one iteration is one review and the implementer's answer to each finding. A change is not ready for the gate while a finding stands, which is a hit nobody has answered, or one rejected for a reason the reviewer has not accepted. From the second review on, the brief reads only what changed since the last review (ADR-1120 D2). After three iterations with a finding still standing the loop stops and becomes the owner's question on the owning arc, which the session raises in ADR-0944 D4's order (ADR-1120 D1, replacing ADR-0956 D7's ten). The three are the branch's: an increment landed in several pull requests gets three reviews on each. It is a bound on disagreement, not a checklist to pass: the implementer's reasoned rejection is an answer the reviewer may accept.

contracts.title: 4.1 · A change's standing findings are the hits nobody has answered, the rejections no later review has accepted, and the contracts the latest review found not met; a hit answered fixed, a rejection a later review accepted, or a contract a later review found met, does not stand, and a change with none reads ready for the gate.

4.2 · From a change's second review on, the brief also holds each earlier hit with the implementer's answer to it, and the return must say of each rejection whether the reviewer accepts its reason; a return that leaves a rejection unjudged is refused, naming it, and nothing is recorded.

4.3 · Each review of one change is one iteration: with a finding still standing after the third, a fourth brief is refused, and the refusal names the owning arc and the findings that stand, for the session to raise as an open question there; the refusal itself raises no question and releases no claim, and a change with no finding standing after the third is not refused.
4.4 · The command line and the agent link's tools record the same answer to a hit and give the same standing findings, each through this package's public API.

4.5 · From a change's second review on, a brief read from its worktree holds only the diff since the last review taken, naming that review, while its packages stay the whole change's; once the branch has taken in its default branch since, the brief holds the whole diff again.

4.6 · A change's three reviews are its branch's: a review whose commit its default branch has since taken in (an earlier merged pull request's of the same increment), or whose commit the repository does not hold at all (another repository's, as a branch rebuilt in a fresh history finds), does not count toward the three, while one branch still stops at three
4.7 · A contract finding stands only while the increment still names its contract
4.8 · An accepted rejection is not re-taken by a later review

capabilities.title: 5 · Graduation
capabilities.description: Graduating a check moves all of it, or the part of it that is a fixed pattern, from the reviewer to a deterministic check in Guardrails (ADR-0956 D5). The check's record says which part graduated and where it is now enforced; the part that still needs judgement stays with the reviewer. Guardrails does not reach the library, so this story runs Guardrails' graduated checks on the change under review and records what they find in the QA ledger, under the check each graduated from.

contracts.title: 5.1 · Graduating a check, whole or in part, writes on its record which part graduated and the Guardrails check that now enforces it, and the checks reading shows both; naming a Guardrails check that does not exist is refused, and nothing is written.
5.2 · A check graduated whole is no longer in the review brief; one graduated in part stays in it with the graduated part named, so the reviewer judges only the rest.

5.3 · Recording a review also records what Guardrails' graduated checks find on the same change: each as ran, with each hit, under the check it graduated from, by project and package, marked as the graduated check's and not the reviewer's; the ledger's reading counts them under that check.

capabilities.title: 6 · Risk reading
capabilities.description: Reads a change's risk line (tier, rating, depth, radius, flags, stories) from its diff and the package graph, and each story's standing risk reading from its package's code, deterministically (question_1740edf77e9e, question_0f21964e8ce0).

contracts.title: 6.1 · A change's risk line is read from its diff and the package graph
6.2 · Each story's standing risk reading is read from its package's code and its place in the graph
6.3 · `quality risk` writes an increment's risk line, and `quality story-risks` every story's reading, each run as a write, so its history entries name the session or person who ran it
6.4 · `quality story-risks` writes no history for a story whose reading has not changed since its last run, whatever day it is read

capabilities.title: 7 · Mutation report
capabilities.description: Each change gets a small mutation report (ADR-1153 D1): at most one deliberate break per changed line, about 15 at most, run against only the tests that reach the line's file; arid lines are left out, and each break no test notices is a hit recorded with the review, ranked by what depends on its file. It never blocks a merge.

contracts.title: 7.1 · A change's breaks are at most one per changed source line, about 15 in all spread across them, and none on an arid line: a logging or output call, an upper-case constant's setting, or a line on the arid list

7.2 · Each break runs against only the tests that reach its file; one no test notices survives, ranked by how many files depend on its file, a file no test reaches survives untried, and tests that fail unbroken are left out, a break with none left not run and said so

7.3 · The brief read from a change's worktree carries its mutation report, and taking that review's return records each survivor as a hit found by the mutation report, which the implementer answers like any other

7.4 · A rejected survivor's line joins the arid list and is not offered again, and the rejection stands without a reviewer accepting it, so the report never holds a change back; a report that cannot run says why and never refuses a brief

7.5 · A break its own package's tests miss, or cannot judge because they all fail unbroken, is run against the tests downstream that reach its file before it is called a survivor; one those tests cannot judge either, or the report's time runs out on, is not run, never a survivor
7.6 · A break is caught when a test that passed with nothing broken no longer passes with it planted, so a test failing unbroken leaves out only itself, not the other tests in its file
7.8 · A report never changes the checkout it is given: its breaks are planted in a copy, and a killed report's copy is removed by the next one
7.9 · A killed report's throwaway Postgres is stopped, and its folder removed, by the next report

7.10 · The brief's mutation report also runs on each outside checkout it reads, a factory worktree or an --also checkout, its survivors recorded as hits with the review, or says why it did not run there

reported.note: passing with the change

contracts.title: 7.11 · A line the change adds exactly as a line it deletes, in its own diff or an outside checkout's, gets no break; the lines it edited still do

capabilities.title: 8 · Verified test run
capabilities.description: storytree runs a project's test command itself and records the result against the folder's files, so the next role in a user's build loop (the orchestrator after the green builder, the reviewer) reads that run instead of running a slow suite again.

contracts.title: 8.1 · run_tests runs the command in the folder and records its exit code, time and last lines against the folder's files and the command, answering passed or failed with them

8.2 · run_tests with the same command at the same files, committed or not, answers from the recorded run, naming who ran it and when, without running it; an edited or new file, another command, or fresh runs it again
8.3 · run_tests in a folder outside any Git repository is refused, saying why, with nothing run

8.4 · storytree run-tests <command> [--fresh], with no library or MCP server, runs and records the same verified run as run_tests and prints its answer; a run either door recorded at the same files and command is answered by the other without running it; outside a Git repository it is refused, saying why

stories.title: The MCP server
stories.description: The MCP server is the second front door: the tool server an agent's harness starts, which serves every story's work as tools through one wrapper (routing the folder, naming the calling session, recording the call, ending merged claims) and hands the agent the habits card naming exactly those tools. It depends on every story it serves, and no story depends on it.

depth.reason: no depth flag in its code

radius.reason: 1 package downstream; no audience of its own or downstream, so owner

capabilities.title: 6 · Agent tools (the MCP server)
capabilities.description:
The toolbox the agent calls, served as an MCP server: plan work (arc, story, capability, contract), see the plan and who is on what, claim or release a capability, report a contract red or green, report a capability landed, say a capability is built so it is no longer proposed (`mark_built`, ADR-0744 D2), and search, read and write artifacts (plus list and add a node's front covers, once the library has them). Each tool is a thin wrapper over the library API and the claims above that answers in a short plain sentence the agent can act on, and every artifact read is logged in the agent activity log (ADR-0624); a new artifact with no place named goes onto the claimed capability's shelf of front covers (ADR-0627 D4, which redirected ADR-0624's default link).

As built: the 6.21 MCP cancellation checks cover claim, make_workspace and attach_workspace before and after library admission. They wait for their blocking and observing database connections to disconnect before removing the throwaway project. An admitted claim still finishes normally; this corrects the test teardown, not the cancellation contract.

contracts.title: 6.1 · A test client talks to the server inside the test itself, with no real agent and no network. It lists the tools, then plans an arc, a story, a capability and a contract, which then appear in the library's tree, the story and the capability each with its founding decision as the first book on its shelf, and it can correct each of them.

6.2 · It claims the capability and the increment it drives, sees both named with their holders in the plan and its data, reports the contract red and then green (the library shows the agent's report going from failing to passing, while the verified column stays "not checked"), and reports the capability landed, which ends the claim.
6.3 · Every call is recorded against the session that made it, using the session id the harness passes, and the machine it ran on.

6.4 · A bad call, such as an unknown capability, gets a readable refusal rather than a crash, and with storytree stopped every tool answers "storytree isn't running, carry on without it". If the database accepts TCP but never completes a fresh handshake, a tool call gives up at the 3-second connection deadline, including its library open, and says storytree is not reachable with what to check before retrying. A later call on the same tool server recovers when the database answers.

6.5 · An artifact written with no place named while holding a capability claim goes onto that capability's shelf as ADR-0627 D4 says, even with a newer increment claim; one with no capability claim gets no default place.

6.6 · Searching and opening an artifact leaves a log line saying which session read it, how it was found (a search result, a link from another artifact, by id, or from a shelf) and whether it took a peek or the whole artifact.

6.7 · Each read also names the agent that made it: a subagent by its id, type and task, or the orchestrator, as the harness revealed them (Claude Code through the hook's line for the call, Codex on the call itself), and "unknown" for a call the harness said nothing about.

6.8 · After Claude Code's `/clear`, which gives the window a new session id the tool server never sees, each call is recorded on the new session, as the hook before it named it; a call no hook saw keeps the id the tool server was started with.

6.9 · The test client parks an increment on an arc, starts it by claiming it, and closes it landed with its pull request, which ends the claim; the library shows each step and the arc reads closed. It records a landing that was never parked, parks a new increment on the closed arc, which re-opens it, and parks and unparks the arc.

reported.note: All three committed-write regressions pass, including the real MCP server with a schema-999 sibling and unchanged history on a pre-write refusal.

contracts.title: 6.10 · It sets a wait with a reason, and a claim on the waiting increment is refused naming it; it clears the wait, and the claim succeeds. A wait that would close a loop gets the library's refusal as a readable answer.

It raises a question on an arc and holds an increment on it, which a claim then finds waiting on the owner; it settles the question with his answer, which releases the increment; retiring a held question releases the increments held on it, naming them, and a record that is not a question is refused.

6.13 · It corrects an artifact's wording in place: the artifact keeps its id and takes the new words, only the fields given change, and an artifact that is not there, or a field its kind does not have, gets a readable refusal.

6.14 · It retires a contract and then a capability with a reason, and each is gone from the plan, its history keeping it. An id that is not a capability or a contract gets a readable refusal, and nothing is retired.

6.16 · Every library write made by the tools names the calling session in history, including every record a compound call writes, increment starts, Claude Code's session after `/clear`, and Codex calls made by a subagent. A refused write leaves history unchanged, including a question whose requested holds include a missing increment or another record kind.
6.17 · Another story registers tools on this server beside its own, sharing project routing and the session log, and its short instruction line reaches the agent with the habits card.
6.18 · Another story supplies `land`'s final next line when needed, with none when it is not. A refused landing asks for none, and a failed follow-up keeps the successful landing explicit.

6.19 · It makes a workspace for an increment (`make_workspace`, 5.12): a worktree on a fresh branch from `origin`'s main, where Claude Code keeps its own, with the claim held by the calling session and the way into it named (`EnterWorktree` with its path); for work another session holds it gets a readable refusal naming the holder. For Codex, `make_workspace` instead returns instructions and the exact `ref` and `name` for the app's `create_worktree`, then `attach_workspace` takes that returned folder, ref and name and claims its verified branch. The agent uses the returned directory explicitly; an app registration error with a returned worktree is not a reason to create another. Attachment refusals say the app's folder is kept.

6.20 · An edit_plan call cancelled by MCP while its library write is still queued for the project write lock leaves the record and its history unchanged. A write already admitted completes normally and remains attributed to the calling session.

6.21 · MCP claim, make_workspace and attach_workspace calls cancelled before claim admission leave no held claim, claimed activity line or increment activation. A cancelled make_workspace creates no worktree or branch; a cancelled attach_workspace leaves the app worktree unchanged. Calls already admitted complete their claim, activation and workspace operation with the calling session retained in activation history.

6.22 · A test client calls `read_context` as session S and gets S's reading (session, harness, tokens used, when, source) worked out at the time of the call (9.5), including after S's transcript has grown with no turn ended; after a `/clear` whose hook named session T, the same call returns T's.
6.31 · `search_notes` answers with the library's ranked search (capability 14 of the library story), taking an optional `limit`, and says why when it fell back to words.

6.23 · `mark_built` switches a capability's proposed flag off once the agent considers it built, and back on (built: false), with the session as its writer; anything but a capability gets a readable refusal.

6.24 · A tool call a hook saw writes its `tool-called` line and every `note-read` it records naming that hook's `tool-requested` line as their cause, joined by the harness's call id. A call no hook saw names no cause, and nothing is guessed from timing (ADR-0746 D2).

`open` on a contract shows it whole: its title, its description and the capability it belongs to, as it shows an artifact; `open` on a question reads it whole, with its arc, state, wording, answer and the open increments held on it; an arc still gets a readable refusal.

reported.note: Test 6.26 in agent-tools.test.ts; landed in PR #305.

contracts.title: 6.27 · `correct_question` corrects an open question's wording in place through the library's editQuestion (12.7): only the wording fields given change and it keeps its id; a settled question is refused with its answer standing, and a missing question or no words given get a readable refusal, with nothing written.

reported.note: Test 6.27 in agent-tools.test.ts; red pushed, green on the increment_2d3b0027b274 branch.

contracts.title: 6.28 · `move_increment` re-homes an open or closed increment through the library, keeping its id, lifecycle, outcome, waits and any claim, with the session as writer and the reason in history; open work moving to a closed arc and missing records are refused without a write.

reported.note: Committed move remains successful with its id when its follow-up arc read fails.

contracts.title: 6.29 · `show_plan` gives each capability's word, and for one that is not healthy its reason, who moves it and the contracts carrying it, in its text and its data.

6.30 · health_worklist gives the oldest three capabilities on the health worklist, each with its reason, who moves it, the contracts carrying it and since when, and a failing one its verified note, and how many more wait; a capability an open increment touches is not offered, and one a test run in progress will record is held back, counted and named in its data, and the run named.
6.32 · name_session names the calling session, latest call wins
6.33 · The built storytree-mcp command, started as a harness starts it, serves the agent's tools over stdin and stdout, and exits when stdin closes.

6.34 · A tool call a hook saw works in the folder that hook was run in, the session's worktree, not the folder the harness started the server in: a claim it takes carries that worktree's branch, so its merge ends it. A call no hook saw, or one whose hook named a folder of another project, works in the server's own folder.

6.37 · `land` on a capability whose story's package, in the session's checkout, has a source file no numbered test reaches is refused, naming each file and the three ways out; no landing is recorded and the claim stays. Once every file is placed it lands (ADR-0911 D4).
6.38 · land names each planned contract of the capability that no numbered test in its story's package proves, and still lands

6.39 · A tool call's reads do not grow with the log's length: the same calls (show the plan, claim, read the context, release) take about as much from the store in a project whose log holds weeks of history as in one whose log holds an hour's.

reported.note: Red on main's source (30 KB vs 196 MB); passes on main since #668.

contracts.title: 6.40 · It sets a wait for the owner, with its why and any rank, or an outside event, with a note, and a claim on it is refused naming the note; an owner wait without a why is refused, and set again it keeps the note, why and rank left out; an event wait needs a check-back day; it clears the wait, and the claim succeeds

reported.note: agent-tools-writes.test.ts 6.40 passes against local Postgres. Its red run was not observed separately: the tool change landed before the queued run started.

contracts.title: 6.41 · A tool reports each phase as progress the client receives before the answer, and a cancelled call starts no further phase
6.42 · The close_out tool releases all of its calling session claims, reports the released ids in its text and structured answer, and reports no claims released when repeated.

6.43 · A tool called from a checkout not approved for the project its marker names is refused, saying how to approve it, before the project is opened or any line is appended; joining on purpose approves it
6.44 · Asking the owner releases the work it holds

reported.note: releaseAsked wired into raise_question and set_wait for the owner; full local gate passes.

contracts.title: 6.45 · The tool server exits with code 0 when a delivery ran during its shutdown

reported.note: Red first on the Surface Pro 11 (Windows ARM, Node 24.19.0 arm64) with the old process.exit(0) shutdown: run 1 exited 3221226505 with libuv's async.c:94 assertion. Green 4/4 after the shutdown lets the process end on its own. On Linux, macOS and Windows x64 CI the test cannot go red: the abort is only seen on Windows ARM.

contracts.title: 6.46 · add_remedies adds live friction to a parked increment's remedies

6.47 · park_increment takes an increment's capabilities and links, and edit_plan replaces an increment's capabilities or links after parking; a story given as a capability is refused with nothing written (ADR-0949 D2)
6.49 · stale_claims gives the session manager each claimed increment whose holder is quiet, with its holder and route; reading it ends nothing
6.50 · plan_contract numbers a new contract past the numbers its capability's landed tests already carry, naming those no contract carries; a landed test's own number is kept
6.51 · edit_plan sets and clears an arc's priority, and show_plan lists arcs by it
6.54 · A mounted verb's next steps are named as tools, below its sentence and in its data; a step with no tool is named as its command; an answer with none adds nothing
6.55 · present_question marks a question as being put to the owner by the calling session

6.56 · edit_plan and retire_from_plan, called by a session holding an increment, hold a change to a story, capability or contract planned before it as a pending change on that increment, leaving the live record alone; one the increment planned, or a call with no increment held, changes it live
6.57 · plan_contract adds an advisory line, never an error, when a contract's title runs past 300 characters, quoting the card's definition of a contract

6.58 · import_project imports a folder, given absolute or relative to the agent's folder, into the project as mapped stories, naming each one it added; a refused folder gets a readable refusal and nothing is written

6.59 · park_increment with waits_on parks an increment born waiting on another increment, so a claim on it is refused naming its blocker until that lands; a blocker that is not a live increment is refused with nothing parked

6.60 · every tool call's answer is recorded on the calling session as a door-answered line: the tool, answered, refused or failed with its class, and the next steps it offered as the tool door names them
6.61 · a tool whose door-answered line cannot be written still gives its answer
6.62 · park_increment and edit_plan set an increment's machine to a machine Machines knows, edit_plan's "none" clears it, and an unknown name is refused with nothing written
6.63 · The tool server names every tool it serves

6.64 · check_setup from an MCP client storytree has no hooks for passes as connected, says what storytree does not do for it, and names its session id; a watched harness whose hooks are missing still reads as needing attention

6.65 · A client that names no session keeps one session id for the tool server's life, or the one STORYTREE_SESSION_ID names in the server's environment, so its tool claims and its shell's commands are one session

6.66 · A tool call from Cursor, which sends the tool server neither a session nor a call id, is recorded on the session Cursor's hook named just before it (its newest request for that tool, in the last half minute); a call no hook announced keeps the server's own session

6.67 · show_plan's line for a mapped story says it is mapped, here before storytree and assumed to be working, and gives the story no health reading of its own (ADR-0993 D3); a capability planned on it keeps its own health line
6.68 · A tool call from Pi, which sends the tool server no session or call id, is recorded on the session Pi's hook named just before it

6.69 · plan_capability on a mapped story records what the agent explored with the folders and files it covers, refusing none or an overlap by naming the capability to correct, which edit_plan corrects

6.70 · set_up_project in a folder in no git repository makes one with a first commit holding the .storytree folder, and says so, or with no git identity makes it with that folder staged and asks the user for a name and email (git config --global with their words), after which check_setup makes the commit; a folder already in one is left as it is, and joining makes none
6.71 · edit_plan lets the holder of a capability's claim list it, past a backed-off lane's list entry
6.72 · search_notes says each friction report's state, so a settled one found by meaning reads as settled
6.73 · plan_contract's reply names the capability's other contracts that no numbered test carries yet, so a lane reuses a backed-off lane's promise instead of planning a duplicate

6.74 · import_project on a folder already imported says the commit recorded before and now (or that it did not move), counts the files added, changed and removed between them, naming up to ten of each, and names each explored capability whose files are gone as left for an agent

6.75 · The tool server mounts the tool parts its story packages' manifests name (`#parts/tools`): the librarian's, then quality assurance's, then Session management's hook event tool and its claim, context and runs tools, then the map's, then App setup's, each given the project served and the server's tool names
6.76 · A mounted verb's optional text input may be left out of its tool call
6.77 · A mounted verb's many and fields inputs are served as a list and an object
6.78 · A mounted verb's count input is a whole number above 0 in its tool call, left out only when optional, and its fields input marked json an optional object of any values

6.79 · The tool server takes a hook event from a harness through its hook_event tool, mounted from Session management's manifest, and records it through its own connection with no tool-called or door-answered line; the habits card does not name it

6.90 · A tool the lane's experiment arm denies does nothing else: it answers as refused, saying which experiment and arm deny it, and is recorded as a door-answered line with outcome denied-by-arm carrying the experiment and arm (ADR-1064 D2).
6.91 · The claim tool takes several capabilities with one reason, all or nothing
6.92 · show_plan lists live arcs and those closed yesterday or today; given closed (today, yesterday, week) or from and to, only the arcs closed in that window
6.93 · edit_plan on project-anchor writes the project's what and audience, a half at a time, and refuses any other field with nothing written; a story takes no audience (ADR-1085 D1, ADR-1096)

6.94 · show_plan says the project's anchor first (or that it has none), and a plan-health line naming only the anchor's missing half, which fails nothing; it names no story for an audience (ADR-1085 D1, ADR-1096)
6.95 · The tool server serves no tool of a story part switched off on this computer, nor of a part standing on one, and serves the rest
6.96 · friction_drain answers, then the drain step's lines on the calling session, or why the doors learner did not run; the step spawns `doors learn` with no session in its environment
6.97 · The tool server opens the project with its home's system switches: search_notes leaves out the notes switched off, and open still reads one by its id

6.98 · With a factory folder chosen and a factory plugin named to stand in for experiments, the tool server serves the plugin's verb tools where experiments' were, and not once experiments is on again
6.99 · edit_plan records the escape an increment fixes, the change that caused it and the story it hit, its "none" clears it, and a story that is not live is refused with nothing written
6.100 · move_question moves an open question to another arc, parked included, keeping its id and holders; a closed arc, a settled question and a missing one are refused

6.101 · park_increment parks an increment born waiting for the owner with its note, why and any rank (wait_for_owner, wait_for_owner_why, wait_for_owner_rank), so a claim on it is refused until the wait is cleared; one without its why is refused

6.102 · land runs every claim check the parts it mounts contribute and is held while one names a problem; with the contributing part switched off, the claim and its landing still work and the check is not run (ADR-1170 D2)
6.103 · With code review and architecture checks both switched off, the tool server starts and serves every tool it serves with both on but code review's
6.104 · The tool server asks the arm checks its parts contribute; with none mounted, every tool runs
6.105 · The MCP server opens each project with the kinds of record its mounted factory plugins declare
6.106 · A knowledge note a tool writes for a session that has read outside text carries what it read in its history; one written for a session that read none carries no mark

6.107 · set_up_project tells the user in one line to commit the .storytree folder and why (git worktrees and fresh clones find the project through it), unless the first commit it made already holds it

6.108 · plan_capability, under an increment's claim, judges the story's capability numbers as that increment's pending changes would leave it: a number a pending move out of the story frees is given, and one a pending move into the story brings is refused
6.109 · apply_pending applies an open increment's pending plan changes under a merged pull request's mark, and refuses one that has not merged, applying nothing

capabilities.title: 7 · Instructions (the habits card)
capabilities.description: One short text, a screen or less, that teaches the agent storytree's habits: plan the story first, claim a capability and open the knowledge it needs before touching it, write the failing test and report red, make it pass and report green, report it landed, and record an artifact for anything worth remembering. The tool server hands this text to the agent at the start of every session, as its instructions; Claude Code reads it from there. Codex (0.158 on) does not: it shows the model neither a tool server's instructions nor its tools until the agent searches for them, so connecting Codex also writes one short marked section into the AGENTS.md in Codex's home that sends the agent to check_setup before its first change in a storytree project and keeps it silent elsewhere (7.4; measured 0 of 3 without, 3 of 3 with, packages/app-setup/evidence/codex-first-session).

contracts.title: 7.1 · The text names every tool the server offers an agent, and no tool the server lacks; a harness's own tools (ADR-1056 D2) are left off.
7.3 · The tool server hands the text to the agent at the start of every session.
7.5 · The card says who decides what

7.7 · set_up_project's answer, and check_setup's in a project, carry the whole card, so an agent whose harness keeps only the start of the server's instructions (Claude Code keeps 2,048 characters; Codex shows none) still gets all of it.
7.8 · The card says what one contract is: a behaviour visible from outside, in what goes in, what comes out and the errors
7.9 · The card says how to build beside mapped code

7.10 · The card handed at session start is composed from the guidance each story package the server mounts declares in its manifest, in the manifests' order, between the server's own opening and closing lines
7.11 · The kept start of the card tells the agent to plan requested work before building it

7.12 · With a story part switched off, the habits card the server hands leaves out that part's section and those of the parts standing on it, names them switched off with how the user switches one on, and teaches no tool the server does not serve

7.13 · With code review switched off, the card still tells the agent to report each contract's test red and green, land and mark_built each capability, close_increment and close_out, and holds none of the build loop's stops for the user

7.14 · With a factory plugin standing in for a switched-off part, the card handed at session start carries the plugin's sections in the part's place, not the part's own, and does not name the part switched off; one that cannot be loaded adds nothing and the part is named off

capabilities.title: 8 · Reading the tools' use
capabilities.description: The MCP server's own usage reading: every tool it serves with its calls and sessions over a window of its own door-answered lines, the tool names refused as unknown, and failures by class apart from refusals. The command line prints it beside its own.

contracts.title: 8.1 · Every served tool is counted with its calls, sessions and consumers, those with none at zero and an unserved tool apart; one a person may call is not judged by these lines
8.2 · Each tool name refused as unknown is counted with what the refusal named, and the tool door's unknowns per 1,000 calls
8.3 · Tool failures are counted by class, apart from refusals by design

stories.title: Plugin loader
stories.description: Storytree's own story packages each say in a manifest what they add, by kind, and a host mounts what the loader composes from those manifests instead of naming each story in its own code (ADR-1021 D1 to D3).

depth.reason: no depth flag in its code

radius.reason: 11 packages downstream; public users, inherited from packages/website

capabilities.title: 1 · Manifests
capabilities.description: Reads the `storytree` manifests of the story packages a host depends on and returns the parts of one kind, in order, refusing a manifest that names what its package does not export.

contracts.title: 1.1 · storyParts(host, kind) returns the parts of that kind named by the `storytree` manifests of the packages the host's package.json depends on, each as { package, module, export }; a package with no manifest, or none for that kind, adds nothing
1.2 · A manifest part whose `from` is not a subpath its package exports, or that lacks an export name, is refused, naming the package and the part, and nothing is returned
1.3 · storyParts orders parts by their manifest's order, lowest first and unordered last, ties by package name then position in the manifest, whatever order the host lists its dependencies in

1.4 · storyServices(host) returns each service the manifests of the host's story packages declare, as { package, name, run, module, export }; one with no name, a run but "always" or { every: "<n>m" }, or an unexported from is refused, naming the package

capabilities.title: 2 · Build-time composition
capabilities.description: An esbuild plugin that answers `#parts/<kind>` with a module importing each part the manifests of the importing package's dependencies name and exporting their declarations, so a bundled host mounts them with no story named in its code. Unbundled, the same import is answered by capability 3.

contracts.title: 2.1 · A bundle built with partsPlugin() that imports `#parts/<kind>` gets, as its default export's declarations, every part's declarations concatenated in storyParts' order (the host being the importing file's package), and an empty list for a kind no manifest names

capabilities.title: 3 · Run-time composition
capabilities.description: A host run unbundled (under tsx, in tests and `pnpm storytree`) imports `#parts/<kind>` through its package.json's `imports`, which names a module of its own that composes the same parts at run time: storyParts, then each part's module imported as the host resolves it. The same import is answered at build time by capability 2, so a host's source is one form either way.

contracts.title: 3.1 · An unbundled host importing #parts/<kind>, which its package.json's imports maps to its own module calling composeParts, gets as its declarations every part's declarations concatenated in storyParts' order, and an empty list for a kind no manifest names

capabilities.title: 4 · Switching a part off
capabilities.description: Every list the loader composes knows which story part each declaration came from and what that part stands on, so a host can leave out the parts this computer's setting switches off and say so when one is asked for (ADR-1092 D2, D3).

contracts.title: 4.1 · A composed list carries, beside its declarations, the part each came from (its package name without the scope) and the host's parts graph: each package with a manifest the host depends on or reaches through one of them, and the parts its package.json depends on

4.2 · mount(composition, off) gives a host every declaration but those of a part `off` names and of every part standing on one however deep, and each part left out with the named part it is off because of; the core (library, plugin-loader, project-and-caller) and names the host lacks are ignored
4.3 · `settings set part <part> off` or `plugin <plugin>` names the command families, commands and tools the parts it switches off take away, and those the plugin adds in their place

capabilities.title: 5 · Factory plugins
capabilities.description: A plugin in the user's factory folder, a package with a storytree manifest, stands in for a part of storytree this computer switches off: the loader reads the plugin's manifest from the folder the user chose (choosing it is the one-time approval, question_5867f490cdd6), loads the modules it names as ready-to-run JavaScript while the host starts, and the host mounts the plugin's declarations where the switched-off part's were. Switching the part back on mounts the built-in part again and the plugin not at all. A plugin is handed storytree's interface, never its insides (ADR-1112 D2): it exports declarations whose work is given its context by the host.

contracts.title: 5.1 · A factory plugin named to stand in for a part is loaded from this computer's factory folder (plugins/<plugin>/package.json, a storytree manifest naming ready-to-run modules) and mounted where the part's declarations were while that part is switched off, and not at all once it is on; a kind it does not name adds nothing
5.2 · A stand-in that cannot be loaded (no factory folder, no such plugin, no manifest, an unexported module, no list) leaves its part off, said with why, and the host still mounts the rest

5.3 · A factory plugin's manifest names the version of storytree's plugin interface it was written for: one this host honours is mounted, and one naming another version, or none, is left unmounted with its part off, said with the version it named and the one this host honours
5.4 · A plugin's exported file is found by its export name, and nothing else of the factory is

5.5 · `plugin new <plugin>` (the new_plugin tool) starts a plugin in this computer's factory folder that this storytree loads: standing in for a part, its family mounts and its verb answers, and its own test command passes its numbered test; a name taken, or one that is not one folder's, is refused, writing nothing

5.6 · `plugin check <plugin>` (the check_plugin tool) says whether this storytree would load a plugin in a part's place, and why not, switching nothing: a manifest of another shape, a module exporting no list, a family or verb missing what a door mounts are each said; one that loads is named with what it adds

5.7 · `plugin contract` (the plugin_contract tool) says what a factory plugin must contain: the plugin interface version this storytree honours, each kind a part can be stood in with and the hosts that mount it, a verb's shape and the answer its act returns

5.8 · A mounted factory plugin declares its own kinds of record in its manifest's recordKinds, named <plugin>.<kind>; with its part on it declares none, and a kind it cannot declare is left out with why.

5.9 · `plugin remove-records <plugin>` (the remove_plugin_records tool) lists a switched-off plugin's records before removing exactly those with --yes; it refuses a plugin switched on, and switching off removes nothing

5.10 · A plugin's manifest names its librarian's own database role and update right; storytree fences that role from it to the plugin's kinds, and the database refuses the librarian's write to a core kind
5.11 · plugin fence applies each mounted plugin's writers and librarian to the project's library, saying what each role was granted; plugin check names the librarian's role
5.12 · A plugin's manifest declares its long-running services, and plugin check loads them or says why not

5.13 · A factory plugin that stands in for no part is added under its own name: `plugin new <plugin>` with no --for, and `plugin check`, name `settings set part <plugin> plugin <plugin>`, and every host mounts it, after its own parts, while the setting names it, and not once it no longer does

5.14 · A plugin's manifest names its plan file inside its folder: `plugin check` counts its capabilities, and `plugin import-plan` writes it into the project's plan, adopting a story the first time, saying what it added, edited, retired and kept; a plan outside the plugin's folder, or not JSON, is refused saying why

5.15 · `plugin check` on a plugin made `--for <part>` (or given --for, or set to stand in for it) lists what that part provides that the plugin does not: its commands and tools, as the host's door composes them

5.16 · A plugin's manifest declares gate steps, each { name, when?, command }, which the base dev loop's gate runs: plugin check loads one declaring only gateSteps, saying how many, and refuses a step with no name or no command with why; plugin contract describes a gate step

5.17 · A plugin's manifest declares guidance, sections of the habits card: plugin check loads one declaring only guidance, saying how many, and refuses a section that is not text with why; plugin contract describes a section

stories.title: Context
stories.description: What every call runs in (ADR-1066 D4): which project a folder is, who is acting, and what the user set on this computer. capabilities.title: 1 · Project routing
capabilities.description: The first time an agent session starts in a folder that isn't a storytree project, storytree asks the user (through the agent) whether to set one up; if they say yes, this leaves a small marker in the folder naming the project, and from then on it routes everything an agent does anywhere in that folder to that project, whichever project the user happens to be looking at in the app. It never picks a project by itself: a folder the user hasn't said yes to is ignored, and when storytree isn't running it says so at once, so everything built on it quietly does nothing.

contracts.title: 1.1 · A folder whose marker names "site" gives "site" asked from the folder, from a sub-folder of it, and from a git worktree of it.
1.2 · A folder with no marker, in it or above it, gives "not a storytree project".
1.4 · With the app's database stopped, asking where to send activity answers "storytree isn't running" in well under a second.
1.5 · A leftover address from a crashed app counts as not running: it answers in well under a second and never hangs.

1.6 · With the library set to Cloud SQL, a project folder routes to that instance (its connection name and user) whether or not the app's local database is running, and no local address is tried; with it local, routing is exactly as in 1.1 to 1.5.

1.7 · Routing reads only the library setting: damage elsewhere in settings.json (an unusable context guidance, say) does not stop it, while a damaged library setting, or a file that is not a JSON object, refuses naming the file and is never read as local nor rewritten.

1.12 · A marker alone reaches no project (ADR-0942): a checkout whose marker names an existing project, with or without its identity, is refused until its trunk on this machine is approved, and a trunk recorded before approval counts as unapproved until it joins on purpose; an approved trunk and its git worktrees reach it.

1.15 · Project and caller's routing entry alone (@storytree/project-and-caller/routing) routes a folder: one that is no project gives "not a storytree project", and a project whose app is stopped gives "storytree isn't running", without the caller loading the package's root

contracts.title: 1.17 · Only a git worktree its trunk's repository registered inherits the trunk's project and approval; a copied or forged .git file pointing at a trunk makes no worktree of it

1.18 · A forgotten trunk's remembered approval opens nothing: removing the project from this machine, or deleting it everywhere, drops this machine's remembered approval for it, so its folder is refused until approved again (ADR-0942)

1.19 · An imported folder is recorded on its project beside the trunk, per machine, approved by the import; recording it again updates its repository and commit, and forgetting the trunk forgets its imports

capabilities.title: 2 · Settings
capabilities.description: The user's own settings on this computer, for every story: read and written by Project and caller's package (moved out of Session management by ADR-1025), set from the command line and from the app's settings panel (ADR-0728 D2, D3; ADR-0729; ADR-0739; ADR-0649). Per user only: one file, `settings.json`, in the storytree home (`STORYTREE_HOME`, else `~/.storytree/0.3`, capability 1) beside `project-choice.json`. Each setting has a name, a type, a default and a plain-language meaning. An unset setting reads as its default, marked as the default. A value of the wrong type, or a name that is not a setting, is refused with its reason and nothing is written. A settings file that cannot be read or is not valid is reported, naming the file and the problem; it is never silently replaced, and a set refuses to overwrite it.

contracts.title: 2.1 · In a throwaway storytree home with no settings file, `context-guidance` reads 600,000, marked as the default, with its type (tokens) and its meaning.

2.2 · `storytree settings set context-guidance 400000` writes it to `settings.json` in the storytree home, and `storytree settings show`, and a fresh read by Project and caller's reader, give 400,000 marked as set.
2.3 · Setting a name that is not a setting, or `context-guidance` to a value that is not a positive whole number, is refused naming why, and the settings file is left as it was.

2.4 · A settings file that is not valid JSON, or holds `context-guidance` of the wrong type, is reported on read naming the file and the problem, never read as the default; a set refuses to overwrite it, and the file is left byte for byte.

2.5 · With no library setting, `storytree settings show` reads the library location as `local`, marked default; `storytree settings set library cloudsql <instance> <user>` saves the Cloud SQL instance's connection name and the Google account to sign in as, and reads back as set; `storytree settings set library local` returns to local.

2.6 · `settings set library` with anything but `local`, or `cloudsql` with an instance not written project:region:instance or a user that is not an email, is refused with the reason, and the settings file is left byte for byte.

2.7 · Settings in the app’s gear opens a panel headed Settings, with “Yours on this computer · all projects”. Every setting returned by the reader has its current value, meaning, and default or set-by-you source; values can be saved with capability 2’s writers. A newly listed numeric setting needs no panel change.

2.8 · A refused value shows the writer’s exact reason beside its row, leaves the settings file byte for byte, retains the saved source, and can be corrected and retried. A successful save reads back when the panel reopens. Library location uses the same local/Cloud SQL writer and reports that changes apply when the app next opens.

2.9 · A failed read of the Settings panel shows the failure's reason and Retry, never fabricated defaults in place of the rows, and Retry reads again; a save whose transport fails shows its reason and leaves Save available for retry. The overlay that holds the panel (its focus loop with the reachable gear, Close or Escape returning focus to the gear, and its fit at narrow window sizes) is the app frame's: The app 2.6 and 2.7.

2.10 · With no settings file, `idle-after` reads 30 minutes, marked as the default; `storytree settings set idle-after 10m` sets it, and a value that is not a duration (such as `soon`, `0m` or `-5m`) is refused with its reason, and the settings file is left byte for byte. What the setting does to claims and sessions is Session management's Claims 5.43.

2.11 · With no settings file, `leave-after` reads 1 hour, marked as the default; `storytree settings set leave-after 2h` sets it, and a value that is not a duration is refused with its reason and the settings file left byte for byte (ADR-0754 D4; default from ADR-0758 D5).
2.14 · The app shows who decides what, read-only, from the habits card's own lines

2.12 · `storytree settings set library postgres <address>` saves a postgres:// address (host, port, database, user, sslmode), or a wss:// address for Postgres reached over a WebSocket (host, port, database, user), and reads back as set; an address carrying a password is refused, saying to save it as the `postgres` key with `storytree auth set postgres`, and the settings file is left byte for byte (ADR-0846 D1).

2.13 · Routing reads a Postgres-address library as the library's connect options for that address, and the settings panel offers it as a third library location beside local and Cloud SQL, saved through the same writer.

2.15 · settings.json may name the experiment and arm a lane runs in, and what that arm denies, `"experiment": {"name": …, "arm": …, "denies": {"tools": […], "commands": […]}}` with denies optional, read back by name; with none it reads as none, and a value missing either name, carrying anything else, or with denies not two lists of names is reported on read naming the file.

2.17 · `storytree settings set part <part> off|on` switches a part of the host off or on and says every part now off, each standing on another named with it, and that hosts take it when they start; `settings show` lists each part on, off, off with another, or always on (the core); the core, a part the host lacks and the setting does not name (a factory plugin may stand in for one: 2.20) or a state but on or off is refused, saving nothing

2.18 · settings.json names the system switched off and on ("system-off", "system-on": all, roles, checks, notes, or one record's title or id); `settings set system <name> off|on` keeps the two apart and leaves the other settings as they were, `all on` only clears all; readSystemSwitches reads them alone; a state but on or off, and a name in both lists, are refused

2.19 · a machine's health limits read as 6 GB of memory available, a load of 12 and a disk 85% full by default; each is set as a positive whole number, the disk's at most 100, and any other value is refused with the file left byte for byte

2.20 · settings set factory <folder> chooses this computer's factory folder, an existing folder saved as its full path; settings set part <part> plugin <plugin> switches the part off and names the factory plugin standing in for it, which readStandIns reads with the folder and settings show lists, a part no host's parts hold (one that has left the base, such as voice) included, which settings set part and settings show name; on switches it back on and drops the stand-in; a plugin with no name is refused, saving nothing

2.21 · With no factory setting, storytree makes and uses its own factory folder, your-factory, with the factory's shape and no setting saved: beside its versioned home (~/.storytree/your-factory), inside any other home
2.22 · Switching the factory folder needs no approval and records who switched it and when
2.23 · Switching a factory plugin in a part's place, and back, records who switched it and when

2.24 · A checked-in worktree setup's approval is kept in settings.json per repository, as its commands' fingerprint and when it was given, a later approval replacing the earlier one, and a damaged record is refused naming the file

2.25 · storytree settings set service <part>/<service> on|off turns a service on or off for this machine, saved in settings.json; every service is off until it is turned on, and a name not of the form <part>/<service> or a state but on or off is refused

2.26 · `settings set part <plugin> plugin <plugin>` adds a factory plugin that stands in for no part under its own name, and `settings set part` and `settings show` say it is added by that plugin, not that a part is switched off; a part no host has and no setting names, switched to a plugin of another name, is refused naming both forms, saving nothing

capabilities.title: 5 · Portable user identity
capabilities.description: A trusted sign-in resolves to a durable Storytree user id. The identity-owned Cloud SQL users store retains linked provider+subject identities, the verified email and a replaceable WorkOS user pointer. Proof uses real PostgreSQL persistence to resolve first, repeat, linked and conflicting sign-ins without using email equality as identity.

contracts.title: 5.1 · A first trusted social sign-in persists a Storytree-owned user id, its verified email, the replaceable WorkOS user id and every linked Google, GitHub or Microsoft provider+subject identity; reopening the store returns that same user.

5.2 · A returning provider+subject identity resolves to its existing Storytree user id even if its email or WorkOS pointer changes; an unrelated provider+subject with the same email creates a different user.
5.3 · Authoritative linked identities join the existing user's identity set atomically; an identity set spanning two existing Storytree users is refused without changing either user.
5.4 · Concurrent resolutions of the same provider+subject create one Storytree user and return its same durable id.

5.5 · The server resolves a user only from a valid WorkOS session token and authoritative supported social identity evidence; invalid, expired or wrongly issued tokens, unverified email, unsupported providers or missing subjects are refused before any user is written.

capabilities.title: 6 · Social sign-in and session
capabilities.description: The desktop and storytree sign-in use the system browser to authenticate through WorkOS with Google, GitHub or Microsoft only. The identity package owns PKCE/device-flow orchestration, trusted session verification, session persistence, status and sign-out; clients contain no WorkOS API key. Proof covers successful and refused exchanges plus a real authorized staging journey; production activation remains an explicit owner prerequisite.

contracts.title: 6.1 · Desktop sign-in opens the system browser with PKCE, offers only Google, GitHub and Microsoft, and completes only its matching authorization response; cancellation or a mismatched response leaves the user signed out.

6.2 · storytree sign-in shows the verification URL and user code, waits according to the device-flow interval, and reports the signed-in Storytree user only after authorization; denied or expired authorization leaves it signed out.

6.3 · A restarted desktop restores its protected signed-in session, refuses unavailable secure storage instead of saving plaintext tokens, and sign-out removes its session so the next status is signed out.
6.4 · A signed-in CLI reports its Storytree user without revealing tokens, and sign-out removes its saved session so the next status is signed out.

6.5 · The desktop signs in only with a public WorkOS client ID configured, verifies WorkOS's access token itself against the client's published keys with no identity server, waits for the storytree-auth callback, and refuses a provider refusal, a failed exchange, a sign-out or a sign-in that never returns.

stories.title: Experiments
stories.description:
The owner writes an experiment down before it runs, runs its arms in isolation under a budget, and reads its curves (ADR-1064). An experiment is a frozen record of its arms, hypotheses, measures and stop rules. Each arm is a named switch the doors enforce. It runs against its own throwaway library, storytree home and public repository, and it is dispatched only into capacity the real pool leaves idle. Every merge on an arm's repository leaves one point, and the points read back as one curve per arm. A Harbor task becomes an experiment's work with one import.

Its code lives in packages/experiments (ADR-0649). It depends on the library and Project and caller; the command line and the MCP server depend on it, asking it whether a verb is allowed. The labels on a lane's activity lines are stamped by Session management's activity log from the settings Project and caller reads, so the log never depends on this story. Not in this story: enforcing an arm's guidance, role or review variants; the arm record carries them, but nothing switches them until an experiment needs one.
